Toggle with Kconfig/CMake OPENEMBERCOMPONENTALERTS` (on by default). Detection algorithms, threshold hysteresis/debounce, and reminder periods belong to detectors; the alerts component does not take control authority and does not stop, latch, or recover.

Alerts and logs use two independent output paths: alerts → logging → spdlog TopicSink → log topic for troubleshooting; alerts → LinkPublisher → structured alert topics for whole-machine state managers, UIs, and ops subscribers. TopicSink publishes logs only—it is not an alert protocol. Detection, whole-machine response, and execution arbitration stay separate; subscribers must not derive a fixed stop action from log level.
OpenEmber currently uses a clear four-layer model (dependencies flow downward) for extension and long-term maintenance:
EmberLite uses CMake (3.16 or newer recommended) and, optionally, the same Kconfig → build/.config → build/config.cmake flow as OpenEmber to manage feature switches.

OpenEmber uses Kconfig to produce build/.config. Scripts then generate build/config.cmake, which CMake reads to drive the build. Linux with GCC/G++ is recommended. The minimum CMake version is whatever the repository CMakeLists.txt currently requires.

OpenEmber ships scripts/ember. The standalone openember-cli repository also provides ember. Capabilities depend on the version; prefer the copy bundled with the framework for product creation and model workflows. The framework root provides scripts/kconfig/. A standalone product reaches those scripts through the openember/ dependency and does not need its own copy of the toolchain.

OpenEmber separates build-time capabilities from device runtime parameters. Kconfig with CMake decides what the program includes; YAML decides which parameters already-built modules run with. Products may integrate the framework from source or develop inside the framework tree—this split does not change with the engineering mode.

Robots and smart devices often need to detect tilt, temperature, collision, tracking error, input loss, or communication loss. The same phenomenon may require different responses across tasks: a large tilt angle may mean a tip-over—or a planned climb/flip. Keep fact detection, response decisions, and action execution separate so detectors never hard-bind whole-machine stop, fault latch, or process exit.
OpenEmber 将主机资源监测与网络管理作为可裁剪的公共系统服务。产品通过构建配置与 launch 编排选择服务，Web、CLI 和整机管理通过 Link 消费消息。
OpenEmber 的 IMU 接口将采集、配置、校准分开：IImu 提供样本和生命周期，IImuConfiguration 声明支持的参数及 RAM / Flash 能力，IImuCalibration 提供具体校准操作。产品通过标准 Hardware Interface IMU endpoint 装配驱动，不需要为每种型号重建消息层。

OpenEmber is a runtime framework for robotics and intelligent devices on Linux. It provides a unified communication backbone, a hardware abstraction layer (HAL), and a node execution model for building distributed embedded systems.

OpenEmber separates process lifecycle from product state. By default launchmanager creates a local Link router and ordinary nodes join as clients; standalone debug programs may create their own router. Whole-machine state management is a separate service: shared aggregation lives in components/systemstate, while model rules and execution logic belong to the product.

components/algorithm is OpenEmber's lightweight general-purpose algorithm library for the high-frequency primitives used in intelligent devices, robots, and edge runtimes.

OpenEmber Link is the stable communication layer for nodes, tools, system services, and device management. Upward it provides topics, services, liveliness, node discovery, and diagnostics. Downward it hides the concrete middleware. Application code should program against OpenEmber communication semantics, not against Zenoh mode, endpoint, key expression, or session details.
components/logging is OpenEmber's in-process logging component. The C++ API is openember::Logger. Application code keeps using the LOG and OE_LOG macros.

openember-msgs is the message-protocol repository shared by OpenEmber and EmberLite. It stores .proto definitions, Nanopb constraints, and the generation entry points. It does not implement the OpenEmber or EmberLite runtime.

components/thread_pool is OpenEmber's fixed-size thread pool. Use it to run short tasks asynchronously inside a node (for example parsing inside a message callback, or non-real-time post-processing) without blocking the main loop or a communication thread.

OpenEmber supports three engineering modes: maintain the framework source tree directly, integrate the framework source into an independent product and build together, and—planned—develop against an installed SDK. The first two already have entry points; the third is for later SDK delivery.

RBU (Robot Bundle Update) is a multi-component release description and update-bundle format for robots and complex intelligent devices. It aggregates, describes, verifies, and orchestrates update artifacts. It does not replace Debian packages, a Linux image, or an MCU firmware format.

C keeps call graphs and resource usage easier to reason about and aligns well with MISRA-style rules. EmberLite is not meant to replace ROS2 or OpenEmber—it gives resource-constrained embedded Linux devices a lightweight node model and pub/sub messaging while staying on the same Kconfig + CMake and ember CLI workflow, so teams can switch repos without relearning tooling. Read more in the Introduction.

OpenEmber core components/alerts provides in-process alert state, an event queue, and async log dispatch. CMake target openember::alerts, header <openember/alerts/manager.hpp>. Toggle with Kconfig/CMake OPENEMBER_COMPONENT_ALERTS (on by default). Detection algorithms, threshold hysteresis/debounce, and reminder periods belong to detectors; the alerts component does not take control authority and does not stop, latch, or recover.

Event.key identifies a condition via source module, device, session, and alert code. Raised, Reminder, Cleared, and Unknown record condition active, sustained reminder, clear, and cannot-judge. Severity is independently Severity::Warning or Severity::Error—severity does not imply a whole-machine action. Snapshot() returns the last accepted event per condition; Reminder means still active; Unknown is not healthy. Snapshots keep original sample times; consumers check freshness. Stopping detection does not auto-claim conditions cleared. Events carry sample sequence, source time and clock domain, duration, measurement, thresholds, clear threshold, unit, frame, context, and notes. Within a key, only increasing sequences, non-rewinding times, and the same clock domain are accepted—do not mix host and simulation clocks. New sessions need a new session id; after stopping an old producer call ForgetSession(source, session) to drop old state. That does not forge clear events; already queued history still logs. The component does not decide which sessions are dead—callers must stop old producers. Fields are capped at 256 bytes and reject control characters; key ids and clock domain are non-empty; values must be finite. Invalid observations use Unknown, valid=false, and finite placeholders. Logs use quoted fields so free text cannot forge new log lines. In-process types optionally map through a Link adapter to openember-msgs alerts/v1. There is not yet app ack, durable state, or a central alert service.

Each accepted event is logged on a dispatch thread via existing openember::logging::Logger. The spdlog backend still reuses stdout, rolling files, syslog, and log topics; builtin backend writes stderr. Lifecycle events use at least warn; severe events use error. Clear events also use warn with edge=CLEARED, so counting warning lines alone cannot tell which alerts are still active. The manager holds its own logger instance and sets that instance (and its topic filter) to warn, so a process-wide error-only filter does not drop alerts. It does not change ordinary process log levels or replace the default spdlog instance. Names append an in-process instance number, e.g. quadruped-sim-alerts-1; rolling files follow that name. Destinations, directories, and rotation come from the passed LoggerConfig. File-create failures follow logging fallbacks—no guarantee of disk or remote delivery; topic rate limits and availability still apply. Queue and state table default to 128 entries each; capacity is set in Options up to 65536. Publish() only validates, briefly locks, copies metadata, and enqueues—no log I/O and no wait on slow logs/observers. It still allocates and takes a mutex, so it is not a hard real-time API. Full queue/table returns Full without changing the snapshot; bad data, duplicate/stale events, and post-stop submits return Invalid, Stale, and Stopped. All rejects are counted; the live dispatch thread periodically warns with reject totals. Callers must check the result or watch Stats()—do not treat rejects as successful reports. Submits after stop only increment counters; the dispatch thread has already ended. Options.observer receives events after the log call, on the dispatch thread, for local subscribers. The dedicated Link adapter uses a bounded event history and does not depend on this callback. Callbacks must return in bounded time and must not call Stop() or destroy the same manager. Callback exceptions are isolated into dispatch_errors and do not kill the dispatch thread. Stats().delivered is completed dispatch attempts, not storage/network ack; dispatch_errors counts exceptions thrown back to the caller; errors handled inside logging still follow logging rules.

openember::alerts::Options options; options.logging = openember::logging::LoggerConfig::from_build_defaults("robot-alerts"); openember::alerts::Manager alerts(std::move(options)); openember::alerts::Event event; event.key = {"motion", "robot-1", "session-1", "tilt"}; event.sequence = 1; event.time_ns = 1000000000; event.clock_domain = "simulation"; event.value = 0.8; event.threshold = 0.7; event.clear_threshold = 0.6; event.unit = "rad"; event.context = "locomotion"; const auto result = alerts.Publish(std::move(event)); // Consume result / Stats(); the product decides motion response separately. // Stop producers first, then drain and join outside the control loop. alerts.Stop(); Construction starts the dispatch thread; failure to init the log backend fails construction. Stop() closes intake, drains accepted events, and joins; it is idempotent and also runs from the destructor. Slow logs/callbacks can extend drain time—stop/destroy outside control threads. v1 is bounded in-process dispatch only; the queue is not durable across crash or power loss.

The quadruped pure-threshold detector stays in quadruped_policy and emits tilt / low-root-height events from YAML. The runner maps them to openember::alerts::Event with source quadruped.policy, keeping sim time, session, units, and action context for the core log thread. The window still shows TILT WARNING or LOW HEIGHT WARNING; the product explicitly uses report_only. On R reset, stop the old control session, drop that session’s alert snapshot, and create a new session; alerts do not affect independent physics stepping.

Core tests alerts_lifecycle, alerts_validation, alerts_capacity, and alerts_async cover lifecycle, sample order, clock domains, invalid data, capacity, slow consumers, callback exceptions, and stop drain. With the spdlog backend, alerts_logging checks warning/error file records, clear markers, sample metadata, and that an error-only input config does not swallow warning alerts. Structured alert publishing, topics, heartbeats, and whole-machine consumer rules: Alert events and Link.

Alerts and logs use two independent output paths: alerts → logging → spdlog TopicSink → log topic for troubleshooting; alerts → LinkPublisher → structured alert topics for whole-machine state managers, UIs, and ops subscribers. TopicSink publishes logs only—it is not an alert protocol. Detection, whole-machine response, and execution arbitration stay separate; subscribers must not derive a fixed stop action from log level.

Enable OPENEMBER_COMPONENT_ALERTS_LINK for target openember::alerts_link and header <openember/alerts/link_publisher.hpp>. It depends on OPENEMBER_COMPONENT_ALERTS, Link, and the openember-msgs alerts/v1 contract. Core leaves this optional adapter off by default; the quadruped host product enables it explicitly. Missing message support fails configure—you need a message repo with OPENEMBER_ALERTS_CONTRACT_VERSION=1. Pure in-process alerts do not require Link or protobuf. Public protos live in openember-msgs/proto/openember/msgs/alerts/v1/alerts.proto: AlertEvent is one accepted condition change or reminder; AlertState is a full snapshot for one publisher instance. Payloads are protobuf on OpenEmber Node typed pub/sub—independent of the JSON log topic. Logical topic Message Content /alerts/events openember.msgs.alerts.v1.AlertEvent Raise, reminder, clear, unknown + sample metadata /alerts/state openember.msgs.alerts.v1.AlertState Full condition table, revision, heartbeat, online flag, dispatch stats /openember/log Existing JSON logs warning/error text from logging TopicSink The first two topics are in the Node’s communication scope. With an empty default namespace and robot_id P05W_C0_HW1D0, underlying keys are openember/P05W_C0_HW1D0/topics/alerts/events and .../alerts/state. Subscribers must use the same robot_id and namespace; LinkOptions.robot_id also fills the protocol Header—keep it consistent with Context. Existing log TopicSink keeps its own Context, robot_id openember, and fixed local connect options; adding the alert adapter does not migrate that scope.

When Manager accepts an event it synchronously updates the log queue, bounded event history, and state table—no network or log I/O. History defaults to 128 entries via Options.history_capacity, independent of the log queue. ReadSince(revision) returns a consistent delta history, current state, stats, and revision under a short lock. Each accepted event bumps a global revision; ForgetSession also bumps revision when state is actually removed, without forging clears. Snapshots include all last observations, including cleared conditions; REMINDER means still active; UNKNOWN is not healthy. LinkPublisher runs its own thread: by default check history every 20 ms, publish a full snapshot every 1 s, and also publish immediately on state change. It does not call the log sink and does not use Options.observer, so blocked log writes/topics/observers do not block Link dispatch of already-accepted events. When the log queue or state table is full, Manager may still reject new submits—rejected events enter neither channel; monitor reject counts. Pass a live Manager, Node, and LinkOptions into the adapter; failure to create communication resources fails construction. Stop order: stop event producers → LinkPublisher::Stop() → Manager::Stop() → close Context. Before the adapter stops it reads current state once and tries to publish online=false; destruction also Stop()s. Manager, Node, and Context must outlive the adapter—do not destroy them from the publisher thread. Link send failures only increment counters and do not change control authority; periodic snapshots keep retrying. openember::alerts::Manager alerts; // context already Init; runtime.robot_id matches link_options.robot_id. auto node = std::make_shared<openember::Node>(context, "motion_alerts"); openember::alerts::LinkOptions link_options; link_options.robot_id = "robot-1"; openember::alerts::LinkPublisher publisher(alerts, node, link_options); // Detectors call alerts.Publish(event); logging and Link dispatch separately. // After stopping detectors: publisher.Stop(); alerts.Stop();

Each adapter lifetime creates a new publisher_instance. Within one instance, revision is monotonic. Event sample sequences still belong to the original detection condition—do not mix them with revision. Header Unix time is when the network message was produced; observation.sample_time_ns belongs to an explicit clock_domain. Simulation pause does not advance source time, but Link heartbeats still follow host time. Publisher heartbeat only proves the state publisher is online—not that every detector is still sampling. Consumers must also use source sample time, detector lifetime, and motion mode. Consumers key data by robot, publisher instance, and condition key. A state snapshot replaces only that publisher instance’s condition set (including empty sets)—never wipe other instances. Older-revision snapshots must not overwrite newer state; a new heartbeat at the same revision may refresh online time. Event revisions ≤ the applied snapshot may be kept for audit but must not mutate current state. Dedupe by instance + revision; unknown enums are treated as cannot-judge. New or reconnecting subscribers wait for the next periodic snapshot—do not rely on prior edges. Do not assume order across topics; a snapshot may cover events not yet received. heartbeat_sequence increases monotonically; default stale_after_ms=3000 should be at least 3× the snapshot period. On receiver monotonic-clock timeout or online=false, mark that source unavailable/unknown—never interpret as “all alerts cleared”. Abnormal exit relies on heartbeat timeout; the final offline state of a clean exit may still be lost. After history overflow the adapter keeps sending remaining events and full snapshots and accumulates history_gaps. publish_failures counts local send failures—not remote delivery. The protocol has no durable events, app ack, offline replay, or exactly-once. Current state can recover via periodic snapshots; lost history may be unrecoverable. rejected_events comes from Manager—zero active conditions ≠ a healthy event path.

quadruped_sim_remote creates a Manager and dedicated LinkPublisher for quadruped.policy pose events using the model robot_id. Default Link peer mode discovers same-scope subscribers; use --link-connect tcp/127.0.0.1:7447 to join an existing router. Link init failure logs a warning and keeps local control/logging; that run does not auto-rebuild a failed adapter. R only rotates the control session and drops old session state—the publisher instance stays. On runner exit it tries to publish offline. Diagnostic tool: openember_alert_monitor (built explicitly when alert Link is enabled). When core disables ordinary tools it can still be built alone and is not in default ALL. cmake --build build/quadruped-host --target quadruped_sim_remote openember_alert_monitor -j4 ./build/quadruped-host/bin/openember_alert_monitor --robot P05W_C0_HW1D0 The tool prints ALERT_EVENT and periodic ALERT_STATE (condition totals, active, unknown, heartbeat, dispatch stats). On observed-source heartbeat expiry it prints ALERT_STALE ... state=unknown. When connecting to a router explicitly, both simulator and tool need the connect flags (--connect on the tool). It is read-only—no control ownership or action requests. Future whole-machine managers should use typed subscriptions and the consumer rules above, combining task, action phase, and other feedback. Core tests cover real router/client pub/sub, all event types and metadata, session removal, offline snapshots, late-subscriber recovery, publisher-instance restart, bounded history overflow, and independent Link dispatch while log dispatch is blocked. The message repo provides alerts_wire_contract serialization and unknown-field tests. Quadruped keeps pose-event, stop, pause, and control-fault sim regressions; pose response can stay report_only without stand-up actions. The new read-only whole-machine state aggregation service is in Launch orchestration and system state; it does not auto-dispatch handling actions yet.

OpenEmber currently uses a clear four-layer model (dependencies flow downward) for extension and long-term maintenance: Application Layer — executable entrypoints and orchestration (product apps, system nodes, optional services, examples, tools) Middleware Layer — communication and core runtime (Link, message contracts, node lifecycle, scheduling, parameters, services, …) Components Layer — shared building blocks (logging, algorithms, serialization, containers, config parsing, …) Platform Layer — OS abstraction and platform I/O (threads, timers, sockets, UART, GPIO, I2C, …) Application is one logical layer. In the repo it is split by role into several top-level directories—not extra architecture layers: Directory Role apps/ Product or user-project entrypoints (framework-owned nodes do not live here; turtle_demo is Turtle Demo; planned rover / agri station are Rover Demo and Agri Station Demo; smart_device_demo remains a minimal product entry reference) system/ Built-in, mostly essential system nodes services/ Optional runtime services examples/ Samples and reference implementations tools/ Dev, debug, and ops utilities Lower layers map roughly to communication/, core/, components/, and platform/. Helper dirs such as third_party/ and configs/ sit alongside. In menuconfig, top-level menus are grouped for engineering UX: Build / Toolchain Application Layer Middleware Layer Components Layer Platform Layer Third party Tests Application Layer aggregates apps/, system/, services/, examples/, and tools/. Middleware Layer aggregates communication and core runtime settings such as Communication and Core Runtime.

You can develop inside the OpenEmber source tree, or let an independent product own top-level CMake, Kconfig, apps, services, and model configs while referencing the framework via add_subdirectory(openember). In independent mode the table above describes the framework repo itself; the product owns its own apps/, packages/, modules/, and products/. Dependencies flow product → public framework interfaces; the framework must not depend on a product’s drivers or business logic. A third planned mode is develop-after-SDK-install: products use find_package(OpenEmber) against installed public headers and libraries and build independently without embedding framework source. Soft-link + build-together remains recommended today; SDK install/export is not implemented yet. How to choose and the concrete steps: Create your first product.

Application (apps / system / services / examples / tools) ↓ middleware (communication / core) ↓ components ↓ platform ↓ Operating system (Linux, …) Upper layers may depend on lower layers—not the reverse—so you can test and swap implementations (e.g. transport or HAL backends) in isolation. Common component-layer capabilities include logging (Logging), Algorithm, and Thread Pool. Communication: OpenEmber Link.

Model device-feedback detection, behavior response, and action execution separately. Detectors report interpretable state and events; product policy decides notify, degrade, recover, or request fault latch from the current action, control ownership, and capability. A single tilt/temperature/error threshold must not hard-bind one response for every product. Independent lower-level capability and authorization checks still run—see Detection, response, and recovery.

Extensible: plugin-style modules and Kconfig trimming for different products and compute budgets. Dependency management: options such as OPENEMBER_THIRD_PARTY_MODE (FETCH / VENDOR / SYSTEM) for offline and enterprise builds. Communication abstraction: OpenEmber Link exposes stable Topic, Service, Liveliness, and codec semantics while hiding the transport backend. Full layered specification: upstream layered design guide and Application layer design guide. Communication: OpenEmber Link. Launch orchestration, the shared Link router, and whole-machine state service boundaries: Launch orchestration and system state.
EmberLite uses CMake (3.16 or newer recommended) and, optionally, the same Kconfig → build/.config → build/config.cmake flow as OpenEmber to manage feature switches.
Linux (POSIX) CMake ≥ 3.16 GCC or Clang with C11 protoc, Nanopb, and Python protobuf (openember-msgs is enabled by default; omit these if the message protocol is disabled)

From the EmberLite repository root: chmod +x ./scripts/ember # once ./scripts/ember build What it does: If build/.config is missing, generates a default config non-interactively. Generates build/config.cmake from .config, then runs cmake -S . -B build and cmake --build. The first menuconfig may download kconfig-frontends-nox into .kconfig-frontends/ (needs curl, dpkg-deb, and similar tools; that directory is gitignored). Common subcommands: Command Description ./scripts/ember menuconfig [build_dir] Interactive menu; writes .config and refreshes config.cmake ./scripts/ember genconfig [build_dir] Rewrite config.cmake from .config only ./scripts/ember update [build_dir] cmake -S . -B <dir> ./scripts/ember clean [build_dir] Remove the build directory
mkdir -p build cmake -S . -B build cmake --build build -j Outputs: Executables: build/bin/ Libraries: build/lib/

EmberLite enables OPENEMBER_ENABLE_MSGS=ON by default. In Kconfig this option lives under the top-level Protocol / Messages menu. When enabled, EmberLite shares the openember-msgs definitions with OpenEmber and generates Nanopb C bindings: cmake -S . -B build -DOPENEMBER_ENABLE_MSGS=ON cmake --build build --target emberlite_msgs -j Generated sources land under generated/openember/msgs/ in the build directory, as *.pb.h and *.pb.c. Those *.pb.c files are compiled into the emberlite_msgs static library for the EmberLite runtime, communication adapters, or example nodes to link. Suggested local layout: Projects/OpenEmber/ ├── emberlite/ └── openember-msgs/ If openember-msgs is not a sibling directory, point at it explicitly: cmake -S . -B build \ -DOPENEMBER_ENABLE_MSGS=ON \ -DOPENEMBER_MSGS_SOURCE=LOCAL \ -DOPENEMBER_MSGS_LOCAL_SOURCE=/path/to/openember-msgs The default is OPENEMBER_MSGS_SOURCE=FETCH. Configure then downloads a latest archive of openember-msgs (currently mapped to the main branch). The build does not automatically use a neighboring ../openember-msgs unless you select LOCAL. If this build does not need message-protocol bindings yet, turn them off: cmake -S . -B build -DOPENEMBER_ENABLE_MSGS=OFF An enabled build needs: protoc on PATH. Nanopb sources, either from the third-party cache or from OPENEMBER_NANOPB_LOCAL_SOURCE=/path/to/nanopb. A Python that can import google.protobuf. CMake tries common python3 paths automatically. If needed, set OPENEMBER_PROTOBUF_PYTHON=/path/to/python3. Common Debian/Ubuntu packages: sudo apt install protobuf-compiler python3-protobuf Protocol design and the Nanopb constraint policy are in openember-msgs.
./build/bin/hal_uart_term -d /dev/ttyUSB0 -b 115200 If the serial port is not accessible, add your user to the dialout group and log in again. More detail: upstream build instructions.

OpenEmber uses Kconfig to produce build/.config. Scripts then generate build/config.cmake, which CMake reads to drive the build. Linux with GCC/G++ is recommended. The minimum CMake version is whatever the repository CMakeLists.txt currently requires. This page covers building the framework repository. Creating a standalone product, build/<model>/ outputs, and the run flow are in Create your first product. Kconfig selects build capabilities. Device parameters that change often during debugging live in YAML. Boundaries and how to read them are in Build configuration and runtime parameters.

Linux CMake (see the main repository) A compiler and basic build tools protoc and the Protobuf C++ development libraries (openember-msgs is enabled by default) Optional: sudo apt install libssl-dev (required by some dependencies) tip The Kconfig toolchain uses kconfig-frontends. Project scripts can download kconfig-frontends-nox into a local directory (for example .kconfig-frontends/) without a root install.

From the openember repository root: chmod +x ./scripts/ember # once ./scripts/ember build If ember is already on PATH via openember-cli, you can also run this from the project root: ember build What it does: If build/.config is missing, generates a default config non-interactively and writes build/config.cmake. Then runs cmake -S . -B build and cmake --build. The first menuconfig may download kconfig-frontends-nox into .kconfig-frontends/ (needs curl, dpkg-deb, and similar tools; that directory is usually gitignored). Common subcommands: Command Description ./scripts/ember menuconfig [build_dir] Interactive menu; writes .config and refreshes config.cmake ./scripts/ember genconfig [build_dir] Rewrite config.cmake from .config only ./scripts/ember update [build_dir] cmake -S . -B <dir> (alias: configure) ./scripts/ember build [build_dir] [-j N] Completes configuration when needed, then builds; also accepts --jobs N ./scripts/ember all [build_dir] [-j N] menuconfig + update + build; also accepts --jobs N ./scripts/ember clean [build_dir] Remove the build directory

build / all default to half the available logical CPUs, rounded down, with a minimum of 1 and a maximum of 8 jobs. For example, 32 logical CPUs default to 8 jobs. Precedence is -j / --jobs > OPENEMBER_JOBS > automatic default: ./scripts/ember build -j 4 ./scripts/ember all --jobs=4 OPENEMBER_JOBS=4 ./scripts/ember build # Lower Rust/Cargo parallelism separately if needed CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=2 ./scripts/ember build -j 4 Cargo follows the selected job count by default. An explicit CARGO_BUILD_JOBS takes precedence. Nested CMake builds inherit CMAKE_BUILD_PARALLEL_LEVEL. An explicit count may exceed the default cap of 8, but it must be a positive integer. Zero, negative numbers, and non-integers are rejected before the build starts. This is the job parallelism of the build tools, not a process-tree CPU quota, and it is not a product Kconfig option. Option forms, log examples, and older CLI behavior are in CLI parallel build jobs. Install options, environment management (ember add / use), and the full command set are in ember CLI. The top-level CMakeLists.txt includes config.cmake from the build directory when that file exists, so Kconfig remains the primary source of options.

Without ember, call the repository scripts directly: # 1) Interactive menu config (writes build/.config) bash scripts/kconfig/menuconfig.sh build # No TTY / CI, use the default config: # OPENEMBER_KCONFIG_NONINTERACTIVE=1 bash scripts/kconfig/menuconfig.sh build # 2) Generate build/config.cmake from .config bash scripts/kconfig/genconfig.sh build # 3) CMake configure and build export CMAKE_BUILD_PARALLEL_LEVEL=4 export CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=4 cmake -S . -B build cmake --build build -j 4 A manual CMake invocation does not apply the ember parallelism policy. The example above explicitly limits the build to 4 jobs.

make menuconfig # usually runs genconfig after you exit make genconfig make update CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=4 make build JOBS=4 # or: CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=4 make all JOBS=4 The Makefile JOBS variable is independent of ember's job selection. Setting OPENEMBER_JOBS alone does not change the job count for make build.

OpenEmber enables OPENEMBER_ENABLE_MSGS=ON by default. The build generates and links the C++ Protobuf bindings from openember-msgs. In Kconfig this option lives under the top-level Communication / Messages menu. Generated sources land under generated/openember/msgs/ in the build directory, as *.pb.h and *.pb.cc. Those *.pb.cc files are compiled into the openember_msgs_cpp static library and linked into OpenEmber through the openember::msgs_cpp target. Suggested local layout: Projects/OpenEmber/ ├── openember/ └── openember-msgs/ If openember-msgs is not a sibling directory, point at it explicitly: cmake -S . -B build \ -DOPENEMBER_MSGS_SOURCE=LOCAL \ -DOPENEMBER_MSGS_LOCAL_SOURCE=/path/to/openember-msgs The default is OPENEMBER_MSGS_SOURCE=FETCH. Configure then downloads a latest archive of openember-msgs (currently mapped to the main branch). The build does not automatically use a neighboring ../openember-msgs unless you select LOCAL. If this build does not need protocol bindings yet, turn them off: cmake -S . -B build -DOPENEMBER_ENABLE_MSGS=OFF Common Debian/Ubuntu packages: sudo apt install protobuf-compiler libprotobuf-dev Protocol design and how OpenEmber and EmberLite share it are in openember-msgs.

After a successful build, executables are usually under build/bin/. The exact targets depend on the modules and examples enabled in Kconfig. With OPENEMBER_APP_TURTLE_DEMO enabled you get the host turtlesim binaries openember_turtle_sim and openember_turtle_teleop (the GUI needs libsdl2-dev). How to run them is in Turtle Demo.

Missing build/.config: run ./scripts/ember menuconfig or menuconfig.sh first, or generate the default config with OPENEMBER_KCONFIG_NONINTERACTIVE=1. Build runs out of memory or the terminal exits unexpectedly: even the updated CLI's default cap of 8 jobs can exceed available memory. Retry with ./scripts/ember build -j 2. If you set CARGO_BUILD_JOBS separately, lower that too. For a manual CMake or Makefile build, adjust -j or JOBS respectively. Permissions: if a script fails with a permission error, invoke it explicitly with bash scripts/.... Do not build as root or with sudo. Otherwise files under build/ end up owned by root and may lose their execute bits. Permission denied when running build/bin/...: check whether the file is empty, whether the execute bit is missing (ls -l), and whether build/ is owned by root. More options and Kconfig symbols: upstream build.md.

OpenEmber ships scripts/ember. The standalone openember-cli repository also provides ember. Capabilities depend on the version; prefer the copy bundled with the framework for product creation and model workflows. The framework root provides scripts/kconfig/. A standalone product reaches those scripts through the openember/ dependency and does not need its own copy of the toolchain. The full flow for creating, building, and extending a product is in Create your first product.

/path/to/<project>/scripts/ember build From a standalone product root, use ./openember/scripts/ember build --product <model>. Run ./openember/scripts/ember install to link that version onto PATH. Install updates the user command link and Bash completion. Both OpenEmber and EmberLite ship scripts/ember; supported options depend on the version in use.

These are the current entry points of the CLI bundled with OpenEmber. Use ./scripts/ember from the framework root and ./openember/scripts/ember from a product root. Command Role new <name> --model <model> Create a standalone product project, symlinked to the framework sources by default new <name> --no-symlink Create the project and leave the framework dependency for the user to add, for example as a submodule menuconfig --product <model> Select a model and edit its configuration genconfig --product <model> Generate or refresh the model configuration non-interactively update --product <model> Resolve the configuration and refresh CMake without fetching Git sources savedefconfig --product <model> Save the working config's delta against the shared baseline into the model default file build --product <model> -j 4 Build into build/<model>/ run --product <model> --dry-run Print the launch command without starting processes run --product <model> Start the model configuration through launch_manager defconfig --product <model> Reset the model working config and back up .config.pre-defconfig new also accepts --path DIR and --openember PATH; ember help and ember new --help are authoritative. --product is a model name, not a product repository path. Rebuild after changing configuration. Later commands reuse the selected model when --product is omitted.

Menu Save writes the full working configuration. If you keep the default filename and exit normally, the config is written to build/<model>/.config and later builds use that file. Choosing another filename exports a full copy. The temporary path shown at the top of the menu belongs to the editing session; on a normal exit the tool writes the real file. ember savedefconfig --product DEMO_A saves that model's existing working config as a delta against the project's shared baseline, into products/DEMO_A/product.defconfig, so it can be versioned. ember defconfig --product DEMO_A resets in the other direction: it regenerates the working config from the shared baseline and the model defaults, and backs up the previous file as .config.pre-defconfig. savedefconfig requires the model default file and the working config to already exist. It cannot create an unknown model. Saving to another filename from the menu does not register a model or change the model id. Adding a model, and the full save flow, are covered in Saving and restoring model build configs.

documents.t: Variable Meaning OPENEMBER_ROOT Force the project root (highest priority) OPENEMBER_BUILD_DIR Default build directory name (default build) OPENEMBER_CMAKE_LOCAL Local CMake initial cache; defaults to .ember-local.cmake at the project root and holds SDK and toolchain paths OPENEMBER_JOBS Parallel build jobs; defaults to half the available logical CPUs, rounded down, minimum 1 and maximum 8; overridden by -j / --jobs CARGO_BUILD_JOBS Cargo-specific job count; follows the selected build jobs unless explicitly overridden OPENEMBER_KCONFIG_NONINTERACTIVE=1 Generate a default .config from menuconfig non-interactively OPENEMBER_KCONFIG_FRONTENDS_DIR Override the kconfig-frontends unpack directory

ember build and ember all use a conservative default: jobs = min(8, max(1, floor(available logical CPUs / 2))) For example, 4, 8, and 32 available logical CPUs default to 2, 4, and 8 jobs. Precedence is command-line -j / --jobs > OPENEMBER_JOBS > automatic default. ember build # Automatic job count ember build -j 4 # Use 4 jobs ember build -j4 # Equivalent syntax ember all --jobs 4 # Also supported by all ember build out/build --jobs=4 # Combine with a build directory OPENEMBER_JOBS=4 ember build # Environment override An explicit value may exceed the automatic cap of 8. The job count must be a positive integer. Zero, a negative number, a non-integer, or a missing option value is rejected before configure or build. A bare -j does not mean unlimited parallelism. The CLI passes the selected count to CMake and exports CMAKE_BUILD_PARALLEL_LEVEL so nested CMake builds inherit it. CARGO_BUILD_JOBS, used by Rust dependencies such as Zenoh, follows the selected count by default, but an explicit Cargo-specific value is respected: CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=2 ember build -j 4 The effective counts are printed when the build starts, for example: [ember] build jobs=4 (command-line); cargo jobs=2 These are per-tool job limits, not a hard quota on total threads or CPU usage across the process tree. Parallelism is a development-machine setting. It is not written into Kconfig or a product defconfig. Version scope This policy applies to the updated CLI bundled with OpenEmber and the updated standalone openember-cli. Older scripts may still default to nproc and may not support -j / --jobs. Check ember help for the entry point you are using, and update it if needed. Whether EmberLite's bundled script supports these options also depends on its version.

When you are outside a project directory, register an environment first: ember add emberlite /path/to/emberlite ember add openember /path/to/openember ember use emberlite ember list Registration data defaults to ~/.openember/ember/.

Command Role menuconfig [build_dir] Interactive Kconfig; writes .config and runs genconfig genconfig [build_dir] .config → config.cmake update / configure cmake -S . -B <build_dir> build [build_dir] [-j N] Completes configuration when needed, then builds; also accepts --jobs N all [build_dir] [-j N] menuconfig + update + build; also accepts --jobs N clean [build_dir] Remove the build directory completion bash Print the Bash completion script install / uninstall Link ember onto PATH (default ~/.local/bin) Full manual: openember-cli README.

OpenEmber separates build-time capabilities from device runtime parameters. Kconfig with CMake decides what the program includes; YAML decides which parameters already-built modules run with. Products may integrate the framework from source or develop inside the framework tree—this split does not change with the engineering mode.

Content Where it lives When it takes effect Which apps, services, drivers, or inference backends are enabled Kconfig / product defconfig Rebuild Compile options, platform/arch, which libraries to link Kconfig + CMake / toolchain Rebuild Dependency versions and source baselines CMake dependency lists, revision / lock records; optional Kconfig selectors Re-fetch deps and rebuild Which processes to start, CLI args, supervision policy launch YAML, interpreted by launch_manager Restart orchestration Device instances, endpoints, sample rates hardware YAML, interpreted by the hardware program Per that module’s load path Joint gains, target poses, trajectory limits, policy paths, teleop mapping Product-owned module parameter YAML First version loads at node start; restart the node after edits Kconfig is a poor place for frequently tuned per-joint gains, calibration, or motion trajectories. YAML also cannot enable an unbuilt driver, install missing dependencies, or override ABI fixed at build time. The sole source of dependency versions remains the lists actually used by the build; changing runtime parameters alone must not switch library versions. Runtime parameters are not hot-reload. The first version of the shared config component provides startup load and validation only—no automatic reload, parameter service, or remote retune. Online tuning during control needs the module to define adjustable fields, control state, full validation, atomic apply, and failure rollback separately.

Core openember::config provides shared YAML file loading, read-only node access, type conversion, and error locations. Modules define their own parameter structs, defaults, field ranges, and cross constraints. The framework does not ship joint names or gains for a specific robot. Products may organize parameters by model, for example: products/DEMO_A/ product.defconfig launch.yaml hardware.yaml motion-control.yaml This is an organization example—the framework does not auto-discover or merge these files. Modules should receive paths via explicit CLI args or launch config. If the product already has a robots/<robot_id>/ asset tree, keep using it to avoid duplicate maintenance. Map per-joint parameters by joint name; when migrating existing robot configs, record source, frames, units, and versions together. Capability ceilings come from hardware/model limits; runtime config must not bypass them. Detection modules should configure “what to detect” and “how to handle” separately: thresholds, windows, hysteresis, and debounce belong to detection parameters; responses under action context, recovery budgets, and clear conditions belong to product policy parameters. Validate and apply both against a consistent version snapshot—see Detection, response, and recovery. That is a parameter-organization rule; the shared YAML component does not automatically provide detectors or response state machines.

Enable OPENEMBER_COMPONENT_CONFIG under Components Layer in Kconfig (it depends on existing OPENEMBER_USE_YAMLCPP). Link the CMake target: target_link_libraries(my_node PRIVATE openember::config) Example config: schema_version: 1 controller: kp: 80.0 kd: 2.0 max_effort_nm: 30.0 Load and validate before creating side-effecting devices or starting control loops: #include <openember/config/yaml.hpp> const auto root = openember::config::LoadYamlFile(config_path); root.CheckKeys({"schema_version", "controller"}); root.At("schema_version").Require( root.Get<int>("schema_version") == 1, "unsupported schema version"); const auto controller = root.At("controller"); controller.CheckKeys({"kp", "kd", "max_effort_nm"}); const double kp = controller.At("kp").AsInRange<double>(0.0, 1000.0); const double kd = controller.At("kd").AsInRange<double>(0.0, 100.0); const double effort = controller.At("max_effort_nm").AsInRange<double>(0.0, 30.0); controller.At("max_effort_nm").Require(effort > 0, "must be positive"); Ranges in the example illustrate the API. Real ranges come from the module and device capability; the config schema is owned by the module. CheckKeys rejects undeclared fields; required fields are checked via At / Get. GetOr applies a default only when the field is missing—explicit null or wrong type still errors. Modules should build a complete strongly typed parameter object first, then hand it to the running instance. The shared reader does not keep a global parameter store and does not parse while updating a live controller. Existing launch / hardware parsers keep their own formats; this component does not automatically take them over or convert them.

The public API does not expose yaml-cpp types; return values are immutable config snapshots that can be shared for reads after load. Errors include source, field path, and line/column when available; missing fields use the parent node location. Integers are decimal only; booleans are only true / false; floats must be finite. Scalars convert by requested type; quoting does not change that rule. Reject duplicate keys, non-string complex keys, << merge keys, custom tags, and multiple YAML documents. Ordinary aliases are allowed but expansion is still limited by depth and node count; cyclic aliases are rejected by the depth limit. Defaults: max input 1 MiB, expand depth 32, node count 65536—these are read protections, not a sandbox against malicious input. No automatic env expansion, no include, no merge of default/model/local files. If a module needs resource-path resolution, define the base path explicitly. Related entry points: Create your first product, build flow: Build OpenEmber.

One product tree can contain multiple models. products/<model>/product.defconfig is the versioned model default; build/<model>/.config is the full working build config for that model. On first configure, tools merge the shared baseline openember.defconfig (if present) with the model default, then resolve Kconfig defaults and dependencies. When .config already exists, menuconfig keeps using it and does not reload the model default every time. Examples below use DEMO_A and DEMO_B. Operation Read / write direction Purpose ember menuconfig --product DEMO_A Opens the model’s working config; on save + normal exit updates build/DEMO_A/.config Adjust features for this build Menu Save (keep default filename) Saves the full config in the menu editor; on normal exit writes back that model’s .config Persist menu edits Menu Save (other filename) Saves a full config copy elsewhere Export a copy; does not register a new model ember savedefconfig --product DEMO_A build/DEMO_A/.config → products/DEMO_A/product.defconfig Commit a verified selection as the model default ember defconfig --product DEMO_A Shared baseline + model default → build/DEMO_A/.config Reset to model defaults; existing .config is backed up as .config.pre-defconfig Menu Save behaves like Linux kernel menuconfig: save the full config or Save As. The current wrapper edits under a temp dir first, so the header may show build/<model>/.kconfig.XXXXXX/.config. Only after keeping the default save path and exiting normally does the tool write the formal .config and refresh config.cmake. Do not treat the temp path as a long-term config location. Save As only exports; it does not replace saving to the default path and does not automatically change CONFIG_PRODUCT_MODEL. savedefconfig stores the delta versus the resolved shared project baseline, keeping the model id. It is not a raw copy of .config, nor only a diff against raw Kconfig defaults. The resulting product.defconfig is for Git, reproduction by other developers, and regenerating config after cleaning the build tree. It does not create a new product repo, switch models, or auto-generate launch/hardware configs. Typical sequence: ember menuconfig --product DEMO_A # Adjust options, Save with the default filename, then exit normally. ember build --product DEMO_A # After verification, update the versioned model default. ember savedefconfig --product DEMO_A The next ember menuconfig --product DEMO_A continues with the working config; to reset from the saved default, run ember defconfig --product DEMO_A. Reset replaces the working config—do not treat it as a casual refresh.

documents.t: The CLI currently requires products/<model>/product.defconfig to exist already; savedefconfig --product <model> cannot create an unknown model. Copy a nearby model’s default, change the model id, then open the menu: mkdir -p products/DEMO_B cp products/DEMO_A/product.defconfig products/DEMO_B/product.defconfig sed -i 's/^CONFIG_PRODUCT_MODEL=.*/CONFIG_PRODUCT_MODEL="DEMO_B"/' \ products/DEMO_B/product.defconfig ember menuconfig --product DEMO_B ember savedefconfig --product DEMO_B Reads and writes then belong to DEMO_B, with default build dir build/DEMO_B/. Copying assumes a usable DEMO_A already exists; after copy, still check model-specific Kconfig conditions and capability selections. Menu Save As into a new directory does not finish those adaptations. These steps only establish build config. To start with ember run, also prepare that model’s launch.yaml, provide hardware.yaml and module runtime parameters as needed, and validate model, device, and resource paths inside them. Creating a brand-new product repo uses ember new <name> --model <model>—that is a different operation from adding a model to an existing product.

documents.t: Host SDK, toolchain, and dependency source paths may go in an ignored .ember-local.cmake (loaded on every update / build), or another file via OPENEMBER_CMAKE_LOCAL. Dependency source versions still come from dependency lists and the actual source baselines. Do not rely on feature toggles left only in an old CMakeCache.txt and not recorded in the model config.

Robots and smart devices often need to detect tilt, temperature, collision, tracking error, input loss, or communication loss. The same phenomenon may require different responses across tasks: a large tilt angle may mean a tip-over—or a planned climb/flip. Keep fact detection, response decisions, and action execution separate so detectors never hard-bind whole-machine stop, fault latch, or process exit. This page defines those responsibility boundaries. Core already ships an in-process shared alerts component for alert state, event queues, and warning/error logging. Detection algorithms, behavior response, and recovery state machines stay in the owning modules/products. The full event semantics below include later design goals—not everything is already a public message contract.

Feedback enters detectors and becomes state snapshots plus change events. Product response policy combines the current action and control context, then control arbitration and action execution handle the request. Logs, telemetry, and diagnostics subscribe independently to detection and execution results. Role Inputs / outputs Decisions owned Detector Valid feedback in; measurements, condition state, and change events out Whether a condition holds; whether data is enough to judge Response policy Detection results, current action, capability, and control ownership in; response requests out Continue, notify, degrade, stop current action, recover, or request fault latch Action execution & arbitration Validated requests in; execution state and results out Sole output ownership, ordering, cancel, and end conditions Logging & diagnostics Consume state, events, and handling results Record, display, report—do not take execution authority Detectors should depend mainly on input data and detection parameters—not teleop buttons, a specific motion policy, a sim window, or process management. Response policy may vary by product, model, action, and run state. Handlers must not rewrite detection results as “did not happen” to fit an action.

Express sustained conditions, condition-change events, control faults, and action outcomes separately. For example “tilt above threshold” is a condition, “started exceeding” is an event, “request tip-over recovery” is a handling decision, and “recovery failed into passive” is an outcome—do not collapse them into a single fault=true. Define severity, actual response, latching, and clear conditions separately. Log level must not imply the same stop action for every product. Condition clear can emit a recovery event, but that does not auto-restore control authority or clear an already latched fault. When designing detection outputs, at least consider: Information Purpose Device/robot, source module, session, detector, and condition ids Avoid mixing devices, stale processes, and old control sessions Sample sequence, sample time, receive time, clock domain Freshness, dedupe, replay—do not mix clock domains in one arithmetic Measurement, unit, reference frame, thresholds, detector config version Explain triggers and reproduce experiments Validity and ACTIVE / CLEARED / UNKNOWN (etc.) Separate invalid data from “OK”; unknown ≠ under threshold Enter time, duration, post hysteresis/debounce state changes Distinguish brief crossings from sustained anomalies Event referenced by a decision, context version, response request, execution result Trace detection → decision → actual execution Pair edge events with sustained state snapshots so reconnecting subscribers are not left with only lost edges. Log with rate limits, edge records, and short sustained summaries—avoid spamming every control cycle. Expired data or unavailable sensors should report unknown / availability conditions explicitly; policy then chooses the response.

One detection result can map to different responses. Large tilt while walking may request tip-over classification and recovery; an admitted flip action may pass through inverted poses while still bound by its own duration, trajectory, capability, and end conditions. Allowing large tilt ≠ disabling detection ≠ ignoring anomalies indefinitely. Run response policy inside a defined control owner with consistent detection snapshots, action phase, control session, and capability info. Concurrent log subscribers and multiple detectors must not each write motors directly. When actions switch, define when response rules take effect—old recovery requests must not keep running in a new session. Blocked reporting or network loss must not prevent local decisions that need to run. Joint/motor capability, illegal or non-finite commands, control authorization, feedback freshness, comms loss, and e-stop still validate under their own rules. Removing “tilt over threshold ⇒ hard lock” does not turn those mechanisms into log-only checks. Local constraints that need low latency must not wait for async event reporting to finish.

Recovery is a managed action with entry conditions, required policy/trajectory, output capability, valid control ownership, timeout, retry budget, success criteria, cancel, and failure fallback. Keep detecting during recovery; stop and e-stop requests still win. New commands, condition clear, or process restart must not silently restore revoked control authority. Products should define what may auto-recover, what needs an operator request, and when a true fault latch is required. Without a usable recovery action, report insufficient capability and enter a clear wait/passive state—do not keep a walking policy unfit for the current pose just because a model can still infer, and do not claim autonomous stand-up capability you do not have. In simulation, stopping control output and stopping physical time are different. After a control fault you may still simulate gravity and contact; only an explicit pause freezes physics. Errors that prevent the physics engine itself from running follow the simulator lifecycle.

OpenEmber core should provide stable reusable I/O conventions, event metadata, time/session semantics, plus logging, config, and communication basics. Concrete detectors live in reusable components or product modules; behavior response, model actions, recovery policy, and whole-machine state machines are product-owned. Validate with real product scenarios before extracting shared capabilities—do not require a universal safety service or event bus on day one. Public diagnostic state can map to existing diagnostics/v1; use existing logging. Model node lifecycle separately from robot motion state. Domain conditions, action requests, and recovery results that must cross processes should be reviewed and versioned in openember-msgs—do not let products copy protocols ad hoc. Existing messages do not automatically provide the full semantics above. See Public message contracts and Architecture overview. Split config per Build configuration and runtime parameters: Kconfig decides whether detection, event adapters, or recovery capabilities are built; module YAML defines thresholds, windows, hysteresis, debounce, action-context responses, and recovery budgets. Configure detection thresholds separately from handling policy; put config versions into diagnostics. Startup load and online update are different capabilities—online update needs explicit apply timing and validation rules.

Start from existing product tilt detection: keep measurement and diagnostics, decouple detection output from response, and let the product choose report-only, end current action, wait for recovery, or request latch. Then add tip-over confirmation and explicit recovery actions; only after models and capability exist open auto-recovery and flip action contexts. Extract shared interfaces and public messages after several real reuse cases. Acceptance should cover different responses for the same detection under different actions, plus threshold edges, hysteresis/debounce, sensor loss, duplicate/stale-session events, blocked reporting, action cancel, recovery timeout, and exhausted retries. Especially verify that “over threshold without hard lock” does not silently enable the device, that “event cleared” does not auto-clear an existing control fault, and that a control fault does not freeze simulated physics time.

The quadruped product finished phase one: a pure-threshold detector without I/O in product quadruped_policy. Tilt and effective low root height support hysteresis, debounce, sustained reminders, unknown state, and session isolation; response is explicitly report_only. Over-limit poses only record local events and UI warnings—they do not revoke output or require reset. Valid initial-state admission and lower-level feedback, capability, and control-ownership checks remain. Product detection events now map into core openember::alerts, with an independent dispatch thread writing warning logs through the logging module; the UI still shows alerts. Events and periodic state snapshots are also published on a dedicated Link channel as public alerts/v1 for later whole-machine managers. Central services, tip-over confirmation, action context, and stand-up recovery remain TODO.

OpenEmber 将主机资源监测与网络管理作为可裁剪的公共系统服务。产品通过构建配置与 launch 编排选择服务，Web、CLI 和整机管理通过 Link 消费消息。 模块 职责 host_monitor 发布主机运行时间、设备时间、CPU、内存、系统信息等只读事实 network_manager（规划） 网络状态查询、授权配置和异步结果；优先适配 Linux NetworkManager D-Bus launch_manager 启动、依赖、就绪、存活与退出管理 alerts 结构化告警事件与日志 system_manager 聚合事实和告警，按产品策略管理整机状态和处置 主机监测复用 openember/services/host_monitor，不依赖 Web 或实时运控。网络操作采用独立服务，避免扫描、重连与权限问题影响基础监测。底层 core 维持通信及运行时基础。已有 components/netdev 提供 Linux 接口辅助操作，未来网络服务可复用合适的查询能力；受 NetworkManager 管理的连接统一经该后端配置，避免多个管理者竞争。

首页运行时间指主机操作系统 uptime，服务重启不归零。 设备时间与时区由目标主机提供，不能以浏览器时间代替。 CPU 使用率用相邻采样差值计算，首帧或计数异常显示未知；分核心保持实际 CPU ID。 内存使用量以总量减 MemAvailable 计算，不能把缓存全部当作已占用。 采集默认 1 Hz。不同指标独立标记有效性，读取失败不能显示为正常的 0%。 通过 /host/resources 发布 host/v1/HostResourceSnapshot。host_id、boot_id 和服务实例分别标识主机、系统启动与采集进程启动；接收方使用自己的单调时间检测消息过期和序号停滞。Web 后端只订阅、校验与缓存消息，不直接采集主机指标。 第一阶段已实现主机监测及产品首页接入，支持 x86_64 和 ARM64；网络管理后续先提供只读列表，再加入以太网、Wi-Fi 和热点配置。网络变更需有权限、请求标识、执行结果和配置回读，并区分临时应用与持久化。修改当前管理链路时应支持超时回滚，避免远程配置失败后失联。 完整实现设计见 openember 仓库 docs/design/host-and-network-services.md。
OpenEmber 的 IMU 接口将采集、配置、校准分开：IImu 提供样本和生命周期，IImuConfiguration 声明支持的参数及 RAM / Flash 能力，IImuCalibration 提供具体校准操作。产品通过标准 Hardware Interface IMU endpoint 装配驱动，不需要为每种型号重建消息层。

启用 OPENEMBER_COMPONENT_IMU_LINK 后，openember::imu_link 的 ManagedImu 包装唯一驱动实例，交给现有 MakeImuEndpoint 使用。采集、参数查询、写入、重连和波特率探测均在同一 acquisition 线程执行；Web 或其他客户端通过消息提交，不直接打开串口。HI 仍负责生命周期和样本发布。协议由 openember-msgs 的 sensor/v1/imu.proto 定义，服务端点为 /sensors/imu/<sensor_id>/rpc，位于对应机器人的 Link 命名空间。 配置是可选能力。频率、波特率、输出字段、校准和持久化选项均以 capability 为准；未声明支持的操作必须拒绝。产品的设备连接与安装参数仍由 YAML 管理，修改设备运行参数不会自动修改部署文件。

认证身份分 observe、use、maintenance，各身份使用独立密钥。使用租约供运控等消费者保留 IMU：持有期间不能配置或重新连接设备。维护租约反过来阻止新消费者取得使用权。产品通过有界的 maintenance_check 回调提供维护前提，例如持续新鲜的电机物理失能确认；缺失或失效时返回拒绝原因。产品必须确保所有动作 owner 在请求电机许可前取得 IMU 使用租约。 使用租约为 2 秒，需要消费者续租；维护租约为 30 秒，正在执行的命令结束前不释放设备独占。网络请求带服务会话、唯一请求 ID 和不超过 3 秒的服务端单调时钟期限。服务缓存最近结果，重复 ID 及相同请求返回原结果，内容冲突则拒绝。丢失响应时查询原请求结果，不自动重发设备命令。 当前传输仅接受本机回环 Link locator。请求与响应通过 AES-256-GCM 绑定机器人、端点、方向和来源身份；凭据文件要求当前用户所有且无组/其他用户权限，建议 0600，创建不覆盖已有文件。日志只记录来源、操作、请求 ID 和结果，不记录密钥。

管理状态同时提供原始样本、安装转换后的样本、owner 会话及主机时钟身份。运控消费者可以从认证快照建立绑定，但必须保留原始接收时间、序号和采集时钟域，检查样本新鲜度与主机时钟一致性。公共遥测 topic 的到达时间不能证明观测采集时间，也不能单凭收到 topic 为实机控制签发许可。 设备读取失败时 owner 保留管理入口供显式重新连接；它不重放旧样本，也不把旧样本重新标成新鲜。设备维护期间观测不作为可用控制输入。产品策略可以选择记录事件或停止，但不能通过修改时间戳掩盖过期数据。

每次写入明确指定 RAM 或 Flash。RAM 只临时应用；Flash 请求保存到设备。逐字段结果包含 applied、rejected、unconfirmed 和设备说明。ACK 或当前值读回只证明设备接受 / 当前运行值符合预期，不能证明断电持久化。界面应分别展示应用结果与持久化证据，不能将 unconfirmed 或仅收到 ACK 的校准显示为完成。 波特率探测只切换主机连接参数并查询，结束后恢复部署波特率；重新连接也使用部署参数。波特率写入的换速、查询和失败确认由具体驱动在独占连接上完成。通用层不猜测协议、不自动更新 YAML，也不以重试覆盖未知执行结果。 静态标零、磁校准等操作各自声明能力与条件；不同设备的校准行为不能用一个“通用成功”掩盖。原生设备只报告已接受时，应保留该状态，完成判断需要协议定义的证据。

OpenEmber is a runtime framework for robotics and intelligent devices on Linux. It provides a unified communication backbone, a hardware abstraction layer (HAL), and a node execution model for building distributed embedded systems. Highlights: Distributed architecture: similar in spirit to ROS2, nodes can communicate via pub/sub and run across heterogeneous hardware (including heterogeneous multicore). Layered design: Application → middleware (communication and core runtime) → components → platform (OS abstraction and I/O), easy to trim and extend. Build system: Kconfig + CMake + FetchContent, with FETCH / VENDOR / SYSTEM strategies for third-party code. Language strategy: modern C++ for the core, with a stable C ABI boundary where targeted C access is needed.

You can maintain your project starting from OpenEmber source, or soft-link the framework into an independent product and build together—the latter is recommended today. A third mode—install an OpenEmber SDK and develop nodes/products against headers and libraries—is planned and not implemented yet. How to choose among the three modes, current steps, and SDK plans: Create your first product.

EmberLite is a pure C, lightweight companion framework for more resource-constrained embedded Linux. It also supports multi-node pub/sub messaging with a smaller runtime and dependency footprint—suited to industrial control, high-determinism, or MISRA-oriented projects (without claiming MISRA compliance).

OpenEmber ships in-tree scripts/ember; the openember-cli repo also provides a standalone ember CLI shared by OpenEmber, EmberLite, and similar trees. It drives each project’s Kconfig / CMake entry scripts for menuconfig, genconfig, build, and related workflows; feature toggles live in each repo’s Kconfig and CMakeLists.txt. Typical usage from the project root: ./scripts/ember build Independent products use ./openember/scripts/ember. Prefer the framework’s in-tree CLI for product create and multi-model workflows—older standalone CLIs may lack support. Build steps: Build OpenEmber and Build EmberLite. Command reference: ember CLI.

OpenEmber separates process lifecycle from product state. By default launch_manager creates a local Link router and ordinary nodes join as clients; standalone debug programs may create their own router. Whole-machine state management is a separate service: shared aggregation lives in components/system_state, while model rules and execution logic belong to the product.

launch YAML supports process args, environment, working directory, dependency lists, readiness deadline, shutdown deadline, and restart policy. depends_on names other nodes; missing, duplicate, and cyclic deps are rejected before start. File declaration order need not match execution order. nodes: - name: service command: ${openember.bin}/my_service readiness: notify startup_timeout_ms: 10000 shutdown_timeout_ms: 5000 restart: on-failure restart_limit: 3 - name: client command: ${openember.bin}/my_client depends_on: [service] readiness: notify startup_timeout_ms: 5000 After initializing resources and registering endpoints, apps call openember::launch::NotifyReady() from <openember/launch.hpp>. The supervisor receives a one-shot notification on a private inherited socket before starting dependents. Without a supervisor the call succeeds immediately. Default readiness: process keeps old configs compatible—it only means the process was created, not that app init finished. Ready notify, sustained heartbeat, business health, and motion enable are different concepts. If a dependency exits abnormally, stop its consumers and recreate them after recovery. On shutdown wait for consumers before closing providers. Restarts use increasing backoff and a retry limit; restoring a process does not restore motion authorization. Timeouts attempt graceful terminate then force-kill after the shutdown deadline. Self-daemonizing programs and grandchild process-group management are out of scope for the current implementation. The OS may supervise launch_manager, but should not also directly supervise the children it manages. Paths support ${openember.bin}, ${launch.dir}, and ${env:NAME}; missing or empty env vars error—no shell is invoked. Config is runtime YAML; which components are built remains Kconfig/CMake—see configuration.

OPENEMBER_COMPONENT_SYSTEM_STATE enables the shared single-thread aggregator openember::system_state. It consumes product-adapted observations, depends on neither Link nor a motion model, and does not drive hardware. Public system/v1/SystemState splits whole-machine state into three dimensions: Dimension States Lifecycle init, standby, running, suspend, resume, shutdown Health unknown, ok, warning, degraded, fault Actuator unknown, disabled, enabled, e-stop Running and warning can coexist; healthy does not imply control ownership. The system service subscribes to structured alert events and snapshots: full snapshots restore current state, events update promptly. Event gaps, stale snapshots, offline publishers, or unknown conditions must not be inferred as healthy. Publisher restart creates a new instance; late messages from an exited instance must not overwrite the new state. Product config maps source/code to observe / degrade / fault health. Default WARNING → warning, ERROR → degrade; fault needs explicit rules. In v1 these rules only change the health conclusion—they do not auto-stop. Later whole-machine requests, permissions, action context, stop confirmation, and manual recovery will plug into the product state machine; motion and HI keep local protections.

In openember-quadruped, products/quadruped-host/simulation.launch.yaml orchestrates a unified router, motion, read-only system_manager, and F710; the default launch.yaml stays unchanged. Enabling QUADRUPED_BUILD_SYSTEM_MANAGER provides quadruped_system_manager and quadruped_system_monitor. The former must use independent observe credentials, query motion read-only, and aggregate alerts. Logical state topic /system/state, snapshot endpoint /system/state/get. Consumers must combine manager_session, sequence, online, and stale_after_ms—do not keep the last “ok” forever. There is no cross-network state auth or whole-machine transition protocol yet. Product build, credential prep, and bring-up steps: product repo docs/simulation-bringup.md. Framework contracts: core docs/design/launch-readiness-and-dependencies.md and docs/design/system-state-manager.md. Local tests cover delayed readiness, dependency failure, reverse-order shutdown, alert gaps and publisher restart, and staying disabled after a real MuJoCo service restart. There are no tests for boot-time autostart or real hardware protection.

Package: openember.msgs.actuator.v1 Definition: proto/openember/msgs/actuator/v1/actuator.proto Earlier joint command / state messages. They remain buildable, but do not send v2 payloads on v1 topics or auto-downgrade v2 to v1. Message Purpose JointCommandItem / JointCommand Joint command targets JointStateItem / JointState Joint feedback state JointControllerStatus Controller health / availability Enums: ActuatorAvailability, JointControlMode.

Package: openember.msgs.actuator.v2 Definition: proto/openember/msgs/actuator/v2/actuator.proto Joint-control contract v2: lease, management operations, cyclic targets, capabilities, and feedback. Full acceptance rules are in openember-msgs docs/actuator-control-contract.md.

Message Purpose CommandContext robot / controller / session / clock / deadline ControlLease Control token and generation JointTarget / JointCommand Cyclic joint targets (no enable boolean) ControlRequest / ControlResult ACQUIRE / ARM / DISARM / e-stop and related ops JointCapability / ControllerCapabilities Joint and controller capabilities JointFeedback / ControllerFeedback Feedback and status heartbeat Enums: JointControlMode, ControllerState, ControlOperation, ControlResultCode, RejectionReason.

Suggested endpoints: <controller>/v2/capabilities, command, feedback, control, and control_result. Send targets only after capabilities advertise contract_version=2; missing capability or fields must reject. The lease excludes stale commands; it is not user authentication. The access layer still limits who may acquire control. First edition is same-host online control: clock_domain=host-monotonic:<boot-id>. JointCommand must cover every joint in capabilities; no partial update; any illegal item rejects the whole command. CMake property OPENEMBER_ACTUATOR_CONTRACT_VERSION=2 only proves generation, not that an HI endpoint exists.

Package: openember.msgs.alerts.v1 Definition: proto/openember/msgs/alerts/v1/alerts.proto Structured alert observations, events, and publisher-scoped full state. Independent of free-text logs and does not prescribe robot response. Full contract: openember-msgs docs/alerts-contract.md.

Message Purpose AlertKey Alert key (source / device / session / condition) AlertObservation One observation (severity, validity, measurements, thresholds, and so on) AlertEvent Event with a revision AlertState Full condition-set replacement for one publisher instance
Enum Purpose Severity Severity (decoupled from response policy) Transition RAISED / REMINDER / CLEARED / UNKNOWN, and similar

Zero / UNSPECIFIED enums must not be read as healthy. Default logical topics: /alerts/events, /alerts/state; no cross-topic delivery ordering. AlertState replaces one publisher instance's set; it is not a fleet-wide erase. Consumers dedupe by instance + revision; expiry or online=false means the source is unavailable, not that every condition cleared. C++ bindings may advertise OPENEMBER_ALERTS_CONTRACT_VERSION=1. Runtime component docs: Alerts and Alerts and Link.

Package: openember.msgs.motion.v1 Definition: proto/openember/msgs/motion/v1/motion.proto High-level motion intent: planar velocity, modes, named actions, and control ownership. It does not encode leg count, joint topology, or internal policy state names. Full contract: openember-msgs docs/motion-control-contract.md.

Message Purpose MotionCommand Physical planar velocity target (does not acquire control or arm) MotionRequest / MotionResult Management / mode / action / cancel intent and result MotionCapabilities Supported modes, actions, velocity limits, and timeouts MotionState Current mode, lease, arming, rejection reasons, and heartbeat PlanarVelocity / AxisLimits Planar velocity and per-axis limits CommandContext / MotionLease Identity, clock, deadline, and lease Intent oneof: ControlIntent, ModeIntent, ActionIntent, CancelIntent.
MotionMode, Availability, Readiness, ActuationState, ControlOperation, ResultStatus, RejectionReason, CommandLossResponse.

PlanarVelocity: vx/vy in m/s, yaw_rate in rad/s; frame fixed by the advertised body_heading_frame_id. Velocity commands always carry all three axes; a missing velocity submessage is illegal; all zeros is a valid zero-speed target. High-level leases are not interchangeable with actuator/v2 low-level leases; clients must not bypass arbitration with joint targets. Requestable modes are only PASSIVE / HOLD / LOCOMOTION when declared by capabilities; actions require an exact action_id match. Successful Protobuf decode is not the same as passing contract checks. Product Link control docs live in the quadruped repository.

Package: openember.msgs.power.v1 Definition: proto/openember/msgs/power/v1/power.proto Battery / power observation and typed resource control. Full contract: openember-msgs docs/power-contract.md.

Message Purpose BatteryState Battery measurements with per-field validity PowerState Power state and metrics PowerCommand Legacy string envelope (not a raw hardware escape hatch) PowerResourceCapability / PowerCapabilities Channel / fan / light / battery capabilities PowerResourceState Observed resource level with validity PowerControlRequest / PowerControlResult Typed control request and result
PowerAvailability, PowerResourceKind, PowerControlOutcome, PowerControlReason.

Numeric zero can be valid; missing validity flags mean unknown, not a trusted zero. receive_fresh is the producer's assessment at publish time; consumers still need their own arrival deadline; duplicate sample sequences must not renew measurement age. Control requests bind power ID, service session, clock domain, request_id, and deadline. Outcomes distinguish Rejected / Accepted / Confirmed / Unknown; an ACK alone is at most Accepted; Confirmed needs actual feedback. Enable and disable authorization are independent; enable_requires_ready and disable_requires_ready describe capability, not proof of authorization.

Message Purpose ProcessSpec Process launch specification ProcessInfo Current process info StartProcessRequest / StartProcessResponse Start a process StopProcessRequest / StopProcessResponse Stop a process ProcessEvent Process lifecycle event ProcessStateSnapshot Process state snapshot
Enum Purpose ProcessState Process state Typical key: .../runtime/processes/<process>. For whole-robot orchestration, see Launch and system state.

Message Purpose Vector3 / Quaternion 3D vector and quaternion ImuSample IMU sample (acceleration, angular rate, magnetometer, orientation, and so on) TemperatureSample Temperature sample ScalarSample Generic scalar: quantity + value + unit GnssFix GNSS fix SensorStatus Sensor availability / status
Enum Purpose SensorType Sensor type SensorAvailability Availability GnssFixType GNSS fix type

Full rules are in openember-msgs docs/imu-contract.md. Summary: Fields 1–9 stay; fields 10–19 are appended (orientation validity, frames, receive clock domain, and so on) without bumping the package version. Numeric zero is not the same as valid; each measurement channel has its own *_valid flag. receive_time_monotonic_ns is the producer receive time; republishing must not refresh it. Do not subtract monotonic clocks across hosts; use local timeouts and sequence progress. CMake capability OPENEMBER_IMU_CONTRACT_VERSION=1 means this extension is present.
