components/algorithm is OpenEmber's lightweight general-purpose algorithm library for the high-frequency primitives used in intelligent devices, robots, and edge runtimes. It is a basic toolbox for sensor processing, control helpers, diagnostic statistics, and protocol checks. It is not a large, general algorithm platform.

Lightweight, no extra dependencies: C++ standard library only. No Eigen, OpenCV, PCL, or similar heavy libraries. Fit for a real-time loop: filters and statistics keep internal state. The update() path avoids unnecessary dynamic allocation. Templates first: generic filters and sliding statistics are templates over float, double, integers, and std::array<T, N>. Component-level scope: only primitives reused across nodes and modules belong here. Domain algorithms such as SLAM, path planning, and vision belong in a module or the application. Small API: prefer small objects and pure functions that node code can compose directly.

Public headers: components/algorithm/include/openember/algorithm/ Main headers: algorithm.hpp # umbrella header filter.hpp # filters: MovingAverage / ExponentialMovingAverage / LowPassFilter / MedianFilter / OutlierRejector / Hysteresis statistics.hpp # statistics: SlidingWindow / MinMax / MeanVariance / RateCounter / FrequencyEstimator control.hpp # control helpers: clamp / Saturation / Deadband / SlewRateLimiter / PID signal.hpp # signal helpers: map_range / normalize / rescale / threshold / EdgeDetector checksum.hpp # checks: XOR / SUM8 / CRC8 / CRC16-MODBUS / CRC16-CCITT-FALSE / CRC32

#include "openember/algorithm/algorithm.hpp" openember::algorithm::MovingAverage<float, 8> filter; float filtered = filter.update(raw_value); std::array<T, N> fits fixed-dimension sensor data: openember::algorithm::MovingAverage<std::array<double, 3>, 4> accel_filter; auto accel = accel_filter.update({0.1, 0.0, 9.8}); Helpers in a control loop: openember::algorithm::PID<double> pid({1.0, 0.02, 0.01}, -10.0, 10.0); double output = pid.update(target, measured, dt_s); openember::algorithm::SlewRateLimiter<double> limiter(0.5); double command = limiter.update(target_command, dt_s); Protocol check: auto crc = openember::algorithm::crc16_modbus(frame.data(), frame.size());

CRC belongs in OpenEmber Algorithm. It is common on UART, RS485, CAN, sensor frames, and firmware metadata. The library currently provides CRC8, CRC16/MODBUS, CRC16/CCITT-FALSE, and CRC32. MD5 is not part of components/algorithm for now. It is closer to a hash or digest, and it is a poor integrity scheme for a new system. If file digests or security checks are needed later, put modern algorithms such as SHA-256 in a separate crypto or hash component.

A good fit for Algorithm: Sensor front-end: filtering, outlier rejection, debounce, hysteresis Control helpers: PID, saturation, deadband, slew limiting, soft start Runtime statistics: sliding mean, variance, frequency estimate, rate counters Protocol basics: CRC, XOR, SUM, and other lightweight checks A poor fit for Algorithm: SLAM, navigation planning, point-cloud registration Image processing and machine vision Machine-learning inference Device algorithms tightly bound to one product Those belong in modules/, a dedicated component, or the user application.

OpenEmber Link is the stable communication layer for nodes, tools, system services, and device management. Upward it provides topics, services, liveliness, node discovery, and diagnostics. Downward it hides the concrete middleware. Application code should program against OpenEmber communication semantics, not against Zenoh mode, endpoint, key expression, or session details.

Simple defaults: an ordinary node only needs a device or robot identity to be created and to communicate. Stable API: user code depends on openember::link and openember::core::Node. The middleware underneath can evolve. Protocol first: business payloads default to Protobuf messages defined in openember-msgs. RAII resource management: Publisher, Subscriber, Service, Client, and Liveliness token are resource handles. Object ownership expresses lifetime. Observable and reliable: the communication layer owns connection state, reconnect policy, liveliness, diagnostic events, and error propagation. Advanced configuration remains reachable: the default API stays small, while advanced users can still set a transport profile, listen address, connect address, and QoS explicitly.

OpenEmber Link lives in the top-level communication menu: Communication / Link Core option: config OPENEMBER_ENABLE_LINK bool "Enable OpenEmber Link" default y depends on OPENEMBER_COMPONENT_TRANSPORT OPENEMBER_ENABLE_LINK is on by default. It selects whether to build the stable user-facing communication layer. Node communication APIs in openember::core are carried by Link, so enabling Link also builds openember::core. Link depends on components/transport, but application code should not depend on a concrete transport backend. Message protocol options live under: Communication / Messages OPENEMBER_ENABLE_MSGS is on by default. It generates and links the Protobuf bindings from openember-msgs. Link can carry plain std::string and ByteBuffer messages. Full node discovery, heartbeat, diagnostics, and the parameter service should enable Messages.

Recommended stack: Application / Node ↓ openember::core ↓ openember::link ↓ components/transport ↓ Zenoh / future backends Responsibilities: Layer Responsibility openember::core Node model, lifecycle, parameters, diagnostics, scheduling, and the user-facing node API openember::link Stable communication semantics: Topic, Service, Liveliness, message codec, key rules, connection policy components/transport Concrete transport adapters: session, publisher, subscriber, query/reply, and low-level error translation openember-msgs Language-neutral message definitions. It does not implement runtime communication components/transport can keep Zenoh as its primary backend, but Zenoh should stay below Link. Ordinary applications should not set zenoh_mode, zenoh_listen, or zenoh_connect directly.

Initializing an ordinary node should stay short: openember::Init("robot_001"); auto node = openember::CreateNode("talker"); Publish a Protobuf message: auto pub = node->Advertise<openember::msgs::node::v1::NodeHeartbeat>( "/nodes/talker/heartbeat"); openember::msgs::node::v1::NodeHeartbeat heartbeat; heartbeat.set_node_name("talker"); pub.Publish(heartbeat); Subscribe to a Protobuf message: auto sub = node->Subscribe<openember::msgs::node::v1::NodeHeartbeat>( "/nodes/talker/heartbeat", [](const auto& heartbeat) { // use heartbeat }); Service call: auto client = node->CreateClient<GetParameterRequest, GetParameterResponse>( "/parameter/get"); auto response = client.Call(request, std::chrono::milliseconds(500)); Service server: auto service = node->CreateService<GetParameterRequest, GetParameterResponse>( "/parameter/get", [](const auto& request) { GetParameterResponse response; return response; }); Liveliness: auto token = node->AnnounceLiveliness(); auto watcher = node->WatchLiveliness( "/nodes/**", [](const openember::link::LivelinessEvent& event) { // node online/offline }); These APIs are the target shape and guide later implementation. Existing CreatePublisher<T>() and CreateSubscriber<T>() can move toward the clearer Advertise<T>() and Subscribe<T>(), or stay available as compatibility aliases.

A short entry point is recommended: openember::Init("robot_001"); That is equivalent to the default runtime configuration: Pick a communication profile suitable for local development. Use the OpenEmber default endpoints. Create the global runtime context. Initialize the Link session, the node registry, and the basic diagnostics channel. Enable the default connection retry policy. Advanced users can configure it explicitly: openember::RuntimeOptions options; options.robot_id = "robot_001"; options.namespace_name = "lab"; options.link.profile = openember::link::Profile::Router; options.link.listen = "tcp/0.0.0.0:7447"; options.link.connect = {}; openember::Init(options); Keep transport details inside the link configuration instead of scattering them across the top level of ContextOptions: struct RuntimeOptions { std::string robot_id; std::string namespace_name; link::Options link; }; namespace link { enum class Profile { Auto, Peer, Router, Client, }; struct Options { Profile profile = Profile::Auto; std::string listen; std::string connect; std::chrono::milliseconds retry_interval{2000}; }; } // namespace link

Link supports openember-msgs Protobuf types by default: On publish, call SerializeToString() and send the result as a binary payload. On subscribe, call ParseFromArray(). On failure, drop the message and record a diagnostic event. The type name comes from the Protobuf descriptor, for example openember.msgs.node.v1.NodeHeartbeat. The Zenoh key only routes the message. Message semantics live in the Protobuf payload. A generic message-traits hook is recommended: template <typename T> struct MessageTraits; Protobuf messages are supported automatically: template <typename T> concept ProtobufMessage = requires(T msg, std::string* out, const void* data, int size) { { msg.SerializeToString(out) } -> std::same_as<bool>; { msg.ParseFromArray(data, size) } -> std::same_as<bool>; }; Users then do not hand-write ByteBuffer conversions. A raw-bytes API can still remain for debug tools, bridges, and non-Protobuf payloads.

Link should generate and validate keys in one place, so business code does not concatenate low-level key expressions. Recommended logical topics: /nodes/<node>/heartbeat /nodes/<node>/info /diagnostics/<node> /logs/<node> /parameter/<node>/get /parameter/<node>/set Link maps those names onto the underlying key from the runtime context: openember/<robot_id>/<namespace>/nodes/<node>/heartbeat The application only cares about the logical name. Differences across robots, namespaces, and deployments stay inside Link.

Link should provide the following built in: Retry failed connections, and let the application inject an exit condition. Return a clear error when publish, subscribe, or service registration fails. Keep callback exceptions from escaping onto the transport thread. When subscribe parsing fails, record the message type, payload size, and topic. Use liveliness for node online and offline detection. Publish NodeHeartbeat periodically. Publish NodeInfo when a node starts. Emit diagnostic events as openember.msgs.diagnostics.v1 messages.

Implement this in stages: Wrap initialization: add openember::Init(robot_id) and RuntimeOptions, and fold Zenoh settings into link::Options. Protobuf traits: let Publisher<T> and Subscriber<T> accept openember-msgs Protobuf types automatically. Link API names: introduce Advertise<T>(), Subscribe<T>(), CreateService<Req, Resp>(), and CreateClient<Req, Resp>(). Liveliness: add AnnounceLiveliness() and WatchLiveliness(). Node registry: build runtime node discovery from NodeInfo, NodeHeartbeat, and liveliness. Diagnostics loop: feed connection, parse, service-timeout, and node-offline events into diagnostics. Direct components/transport samples can stay for a while as low-level debug tools. User-facing core examples should move to the Link API. On a host, Turtle Demo (Twist2D / Pose2D, multi-process loop) is the first place to exercise Link together with msgs.

components/logging is OpenEmber's in-process logging component. The C++ API is openember::logging::Logger. Application code keeps using the LOG_* and OE_LOG_* macros. EmberLite has a separate lightweight C implementation: ember/log.h (builtin stderr, no spdlog).

C++ first: Logger and LoggerConfig are the in-process API. The component name stays logging. Macro compatible: LOG_I and the rest still work. They go through the process default Logger. Sinks: stdout, rotating file, syslog, and an optional Link topic. Not a Platform dependency: OSAL and LPIO do not call this component. The C ABI (oe_log_*) is kept only for legacy C translation units. Separate from services/logger: that service reads log files and exposes an HTTP API. It is not this library.

components/logging/include/openember/logging/logger.hpp components/logging/include/openember/logging/log.hpp # C++ entry (LOG_* + Logger) components/logging/include/openember/logging/log_c.h # C translation units only openember.h includes log.hpp for C++ and log_c.h for C. Do not use the removed core/inc/openember/log.h, log_c.h, or log_wrapper.h.

#include "openember/logging/log.hpp" openember::logging::init("my_node"); LOG_I("hello %d", 42); auto& log = openember::logging::default_logger(); log.info("structured path"); openember::logging::deinit(); Custom configuration: auto cfg = openember::logging::LoggerConfig::from_build_defaults("my_node"); cfg.enable_topic = false; cfg.log_level = "debug"; openember::logging::init(std::move(cfg)); The OPENEMBER_SPDLOG_* Kconfig symbols remain the compile-time defaults for from_build_defaults().
#include "ember/log.h" #define EMBER_LOG_TAG "hal" ember_log_init("demo"); EMBER_LOGI("ready"); ember_log_deinit(); Library target: ember_logging (OPENEMBER_ENABLE_LOGGING).

openember-msgs is the message-protocol repository shared by OpenEmber and EmberLite. It stores .proto definitions, Nanopb constraints, and the generation entry points. It does not implement the OpenEmber or EmberLite runtime. Core principles: Versioned on its own: message definitions are maintained and tagged in openember-msgs. Each runtime binds itself: OpenEmber uses C++ Protobuf. EmberLite uses Nanopb C. Zenoh routes: a Zenoh key decides where a message is published. The Protobuf message decides the payload layout. Do not copy protocol files: OpenEmber and EmberLite should not each keep a private .proto tree.

openember-msgs versions messages by Protobuf package. Per-package fields, enums, and contract summaries are under Message packages. Authority remains the .proto files and docs/*-contract.md in the openember-msgs repository. They are not tied to one demo. OpenEmber already consumes the C++ Protobuf generation target (FETCH main by default, or LOCAL). EmberLite already consumes Nanopb C. The message protocol is a first-class communication contract for the OpenEmber ecosystem. It affects nodes, tools, device management, diagnostics, parameters, and runtime services. It should not sit under Core Runtime, Components Layer, or a pure Third party menu. Manage it with the communication layer of Middleware Layer: Communication / Messages OpenEmber uses the structure below. EmberLite can align to the same semantics later: menu "Communication" menu "Link" config OPENEMBER_ENABLE_LINK bool "Enable OpenEmber Link" default y depends on OPENEMBER_COMPONENT_TRANSPORT help Build the stable OpenEmber communication layer for Topic, Service, Liveliness, node discovery, diagnostics, and message serialization. endmenu menu "Messages" config OPENEMBER_ENABLE_MSGS bool "Enable openember-msgs protocol bindings" default y help Build generated protocol bindings from openember-msgs. OpenEmber uses C++ Protobuf bindings; EmberLite uses Nanopb C bindings. choice OPENEMBER_MSGS_SOURCE_CHOICE prompt "openember-msgs source" depends on OPENEMBER_ENABLE_MSGS default OPENEMBER_MSGS_SOURCE_FETCH config OPENEMBER_MSGS_SOURCE_FETCH bool "FETCH" help Download the selected openember-msgs ref during CMake configure. config OPENEMBER_MSGS_SOURCE_LOCAL bool "LOCAL" help Use a local openember-msgs checkout. OPENEMBER_MSGS_LOCAL_SOURCE must be an absolute path. endchoice config OPENEMBER_MSGS_LOCAL_SOURCE string "openember-msgs local source path" depends on OPENEMBER_ENABLE_MSGS && OPENEMBER_MSGS_SOURCE_LOCAL default "" choice OPENEMBER_MSGS_REF_CHOICE prompt "openember-msgs version" depends on OPENEMBER_ENABLE_MSGS && OPENEMBER_MSGS_SOURCE_FETCH default OPENEMBER_MSGS_REF_LATEST config OPENEMBER_MSGS_REF_LATEST bool "latest" endchoice endmenu endmenu Recommended Kconfig to CMake mapping: Kconfig CMake Meaning OPENEMBER_ENABLE_MSGS=y OPENEMBER_ENABLE_MSGS=ON Generate and link protocol bindings OPENEMBER_MSGS_SOURCE_FETCH=y OPENEMBER_MSGS_SOURCE=FETCH Fetch openember-msgs remotely OPENEMBER_MSGS_SOURCE_LOCAL=y OPENEMBER_MSGS_SOURCE=LOCAL Use a local openember-msgs checkout OPENEMBER_MSGS_LOCAL_SOURCE="/abs/path" OPENEMBER_MSGS_LOCAL_SOURCE=/abs/path Absolute path of the local checkout OPENEMBER_MSGS_REF_LATEST=y OPENEMBER_MSGS_REF=main Use the latest code on the openember-msgs main branch Third party may still contain OPENEMBER_THIRD_PARTY_BUNDLE_OPENEMBER_MSGS. That symbol only describes source acquisition, such as whether to download, cache, or use a vendor archive. It does not mean "enable the message protocol". The user must choose OPENEMBER_MSGS_SOURCE explicitly: FETCH: the default. Configure downloads the latest archive of the openember-msgs main branch. The cache name is openember-msgs-main. LOCAL: use the path in OPENEMBER_MSGS_LOCAL_SOURCE. The path must be absolute, and the directory must contain CMakeLists.txt. The build no longer switches to local sources just because ../openember-msgs exists next door. A local checkout is used only when LOCAL is selected. Recommended relationship: config OPENEMBER_THIRD_PARTY_BUNDLE_OPENEMBER_MSGS bool "Bundle: openember-msgs" config OPENEMBER_TP_LINK_OPENEMBER_MSGS bool default y if OPENEMBER_ENABLE_MSGS select OPENEMBER_THIRD_PARTY_BUNDLE_OPENEMBER_MSGS EmberLite uses Nanopb, so enabling the protocol should also make the Nanopb bundle available: config OPENEMBER_TP_LINK_NANOPB bool default y if OPENEMBER_ENABLE_MSGS select OPENEMBER_THIRD_PARTY_BUNDLE_NANOPB Menu responsibilities then stay clear: Communication / Link: whether to enable the OpenEmber Link communication layer. Communication / Messages: whether to enable protocol bindings, and which openember-msgs version to use. Third party: how sources are obtained — download, cache, vendor archive, system packages. Core / Component: runtime libraries and feature modules only. They do not select a protocol version.

Treat openember-msgs as an independent third-party protocol dependency. Do not copy it into each repository. Preferred order: Day-to-day development and CI tracking main: use the defaults OPENEMBER_MSGS_SOURCE=FETCH and OPENEMBER_MSGS_REF=main. Local protocol development: set OPENEMBER_MSGS_SOURCE=LOCAL and point OPENEMBER_MSGS_LOCAL_SOURCE=/abs/path/to/openember-msgs at a local checkout. Offline builds: use the FETCH / VENDOR archive cache and place openember-msgs-main.tar.gz in each repository's third_party/ cache. Product releases: once tag and commit options exist, pin a specific openember-msgs tag or commit. Avoid: Hand-writing a separate message layout in OpenEmber and another in EmberLite. Committing Protobuf-generated C++ sources into the OpenEmber main repository. Making openember-msgs depend back on OpenEmber, EmberLite, or the Zenoh runtime.

Protobuf and Nanopb generate more than headers. .pb.h declares message types and serialization APIs. .pb.cc or .pb.c contains the implementations, so those files must be compiled and linked into the final program. OpenEmber uses C++ Protobuf. The build directory gets generated/openember/msgs/.../*.pb.h and *.pb.cc, compiled into the openember_msgs_cpp static library and exported as the CMake target openember::msgs_cpp. After core, transport, a node, or a tool links that target, it can include the generated .pb.h and use the message types directly. EmberLite uses Nanopb C. The build directory gets *.pb.h and *.pb.c, compiled into the emberlite_msgs static library. The EmberLite runtime, the Zenoh-pico adapter, or an example node links that library as needed.

OPENEMBER_MSGS_SOURCE=FETCH and OPENEMBER_MSGS_SOURCE=LOCAL can be switched back and forth in the same build directory, but the roles of a few paths in that directory matter. In FETCH mode, CMake configure uses third_party/openember-msgs-main.tar.gz as the archive cache and unpacks sources to: build/_deps/openember-msgs-main On reconfigure, the current implementation deletes build/_deps/openember-msgs-main and unpacks the archive again. That keeps FETCH mode from continuing to use a stale unpacked tree. In LOCAL mode, CMake does not use build/_deps/openember-msgs-main as the source. It uses: OPENEMBER_MSGS_LOCAL_SOURCE=/abs/path/to/openember-msgs After switching from FETCH to LOCAL, an old build/_deps/openember-msgs-main directory is ignored even if it is still present. Switching back to FETCH deletes and unpacks build/_deps/openember-msgs-main again during configure. OpenEmber's C++ Protobuf subproject uses a separate build directory: build/_deps/openember-msgs-main-build The current implementation deletes that directory on reconfigure, then calls add_subdirectory() on the protocol subproject again. Switching OpenEmber between FETCH and LOCAL therefore rebuilds the C++ generation and link targets. EmberLite's Nanopb output directory is: build/generated/openember-msgs The current implementation does not delete that directory when FETCH and LOCAL switch. It relies on CMake custom-command dependencies to regenerate. That is usually enough. If stronger consistency is needed later, add a source stamp that records the protocol source in use, for example FETCH:main or LOCAL:/abs/path/to/openember-msgs, and delete build/generated/openember-msgs when the source changes so generation runs again. If other dependencies later need the same explicit FETCH / LOCAL choice, a shared source resolver can centralize source checks, absolute-path checks, archive caching, the build/_deps staging directory, marker-file checks, and optional cleanup on switch. Today only openember-msgs needs this behavior, so it is not abstracted yet. A heavy shared interface for a single user would be premature.

OpenEmber is the C++ line. Use the standard Protobuf C++ runtime. Suggested build flow: CMake obtains or locates openember-msgs through cmake/GetOpenEmberMsgs.cmake. OpenEmber defaults to OPENEMBER_ENABLE_MSGS=ON and sets OPENEMBER_MSGS_BUILD_CPP=ON in the protocol subproject. protoc generates .pb.cc and .pb.h in the build directory. Those sources compile into the openember_msgs_cpp static library. OpenEmber core, transport, system nodes, or tools link that library as needed. Sketch: target_link_libraries(openember_core PUBLIC openember::msgs_cpp ) Runtime conventions: Publish openember.msgs.node.v1.NodeInfo when a node comes online. Publish openember.msgs.node.v1.NodeHeartbeat periodically. Lifecycle control uses LifecycleCommand and LifecycleCommandResponse. The parameter service uses messages such as GetParameterRequest and SetParameterRequest. Typical Zenoh keys: openember/<robot_id>/<namespace>/nodes/<node>/info openember/<robot_id>/<namespace>/nodes/<node>/heartbeat openember/<robot_id>/<namespace>/nodes/<node>/lifecycle openember/<robot_id>/<namespace>/diagnostics/<node> openember/<robot_id>/<namespace>/logs/<node> The payload is the binary encoding of the corresponding Protobuf message. Type information can be recorded in the node registry, or agreed at the tool layer as a MIME type or encoding, for example: application/x-protobuf;type=openember.msgs.node.v1.NodeInfo

EmberLite is pure C. Do not link the Google Protobuf C++ runtime. Use Nanopb. OPENEMBER_ENABLE_MSGS is on by default in the target configuration. Turn it off when resources are very tight, or when you are building only the base libraries. Suggested build flow: CMake obtains or locates openember-msgs through cmake/GetOpenEmberMsgs.cmake. Use openember-msgs/nanopb/openember_msgs.options as the Nanopb constraints. protoc plus nanopb_generator.py generate .pb.c and .pb.h. Compile the generated C files into the emberlite_msgs static library. The EmberLite runtime, the Zenoh-pico adapter, or an example node links that library as needed. Current CMake entry points: cmake -S . -B build -DOPENEMBER_ENABLE_MSGS=ON cmake --build build --target emberlite_msgs The build environment needs: protoc on PATH. Nanopb sources, from the EmberLite third-party cache or from OPENEMBER_NANOPB_LOCAL_SOURCE. A Python that can import google.protobuf. CMake tries Python3_EXECUTABLE, /usr/bin/python3, and python3 on PATH. If needed, set OPENEMBER_PROTOBUF_PYTHON=/path/to/python3 explicitly. Manual generation sketch: python3 nanopb/generator/nanopb_generator.py \ -I openember-msgs/proto \ -f openember-msgs/nanopb/openember_msgs.options \ openember-msgs/proto/openember/msgs/node/v1/node.proto EmberLite should support both modes: Mode Description Development protoc and the Nanopb generator are installed on the machine. The build generates .pb.c and .pb.h automatically Release Use Nanopb C sources pre-generated in an openember-msgs release, so the toolchain dependency is smaller Release mode is friendlier for industrial projects. A target SDK or cross-compile environment is not always a good place to install Python, the Protobuf compiler, and the Nanopb generator. Nanopb constraint policy: Strings, small labels, metrics, parameter-name lists, and similar fields use max_size or max_count, so the C side can hold them statically. Large collections — node lists, device lists, diagnostic arrays, log batches, batched parameter responses, node endpoints — use FT_CALLBACK, so EmberLite does not preallocate a huge struct for one query response. For a callback field, the upper node or adapter supplies a pb_callback_t for encode and decode, and can stream the data as needed.

Change the protocol in this order: Edit or add a .proto under openember-msgs/proto/openember/msgs/<domain>/v1/. Update nanopb/openember_msgs.options and set max_size, max_count, or type:FT_CALLBACK for new fields. Validate Protobuf descriptors: protoc -I proto --include_imports \ --descriptor_set_out=/tmp/openember-msgs.desc \ $(find proto -name '*.proto' -print | sort) Generate and compile C++: cmake -S . -B build -DOPENEMBER_MSGS_BUILD_CPP=ON cmake --build build If Nanopb is installed locally, generate the C code and compile an EmberLite example. After that passes, tag openember-msgs. Move OpenEmber and EmberLite to the same protocol tag.

Compatible changes: Add fields only. Give new fields new field numbers. Keep the meaning of existing fields. Incompatible changes: Rename a field or a message. Change a field type. Delete a field without reserving its field number. Change the meaning of an existing field. An incompatible change should create a new package version, for example: openember.msgs.node.v2

OpenEmber: Connect core::Node TypeName and serialization to the generated Protobuf types. Use NodeInfo and NodeHeartbeat for a minimal node-discovery path. Record the relationship between topics, services, and message types in node_registry. EmberLite: With OPENEMBER_ENABLE_MSGS enabled, use NodeInfo and NodeHeartbeat for a minimal node-discovery path. Connect emberlite::msgs to the Zenoh-pico adapter. Decide whether a release should ship pre-generated Nanopb C sources, to lower the bar for cross compilation. After that, openember-msgs is the protocol source for the OpenEmber ecosystem. OpenEmber and EmberLite only own their own runtime, transport, and toolchain integration.

components/thread_pool is OpenEmber's fixed-size thread pool. Use it to run short tasks asynchronously inside a node (for example parsing inside a message callback, or non-real-time post-processing) without blocking the main loop or a communication thread. It is a lightweight concurrency utility. It is not a process-level actor scheduler, and it does not schedule real-time periodic work.

RAII: workers are created in the constructor. The destructor stops them cooperatively and joins them. It does not use pthread_cancel. Not copyable: the pool object owns the thread lifetime. It is neither copyable nor movable. Standard library first: built on std::thread, std::mutex, std::condition_variable, and std::future, with no extra third-party dependency. Optional priority: FIFO by default. A task can be given a higher priority when needed. Exception isolation: an exception thrown by one task does not take down the worker. The std::future returned by submit carries the result or the exception.

Project Component Language Notes OpenEmber components/thread_pool C++ openember::thread_pool::ThreadPool EmberLite components/ppool C ember_ppool (historical pthread implementation) The two are similar (a fixed thread count plus a task queue), but the API and lifetime model differ. New OpenEmber code should use the C++ ThreadPool. C code continues to use EmberLite's ember/ppool.h.

Public header: components/thread_pool/include/openember/thread_pool/thread_pool.hpp CMake target: openember_thread_pool. Kconfig (Component → Thread Pool): OPENEMBER_COMPONENT_THREAD_POOL=y # on by default When enabled, genconfig writes OPENEMBER_COMPONENT_THREAD_POOL and adds the library to the framework's internal library list. Main API: Method Description ThreadPool(n) Create n workers (n > 0) submit(f, args...) Submit a callable and return a std::future submit(priority, f, args...) Submit with a priority; a larger value runs first post(task, priority=0) Submit without a return value (fire-and-forget) wait_idle() Wait until the queue is empty and no task is in flight shutdown(drain=true) Stop accepting work; when drain is set, empty the queue before exiting size() / is_running() Query the worker count and running state Tasks with the same priority run FIFO in submission order.

Basic use: #include "openember/thread_pool/thread_pool.hpp" openember::thread_pool::ThreadPool pool(4); auto fut = pool.submit([](int x) { return x * 2; }, 21); int result = fut.get(); // 42 pool.post([] { // fire-and-forget }); pool.wait_idle(); // destructor calls shutdown(true) when leaving scope With priority: pool.post([] { /* normal task */ }, 0); pool.post([] { /* more urgent */ }, 10); Handle a message off the subscription callback so the callback itself does not block: #include <memory> #include <string> #include "openember/thread_pool/thread_pool.hpp" static std::unique_ptr<openember::thread_pool::ThreadPool> g_pool; void on_message(const char* payload) { if (!g_pool) { return; } std::string body(payload); g_pool->post([body = std::move(body)] { // parse / handle body on a worker }); } int main() { g_pool = std::make_unique<openember::thread_pool::ThreadPool>(5); // ... subscribe and run the main loop ... g_pool->wait_idle(); g_pool.reset(); } Reference example: examples/hello_node/main.cpp.

Do not put long blocking work or a hard real-time control loop on the pool. Periodic control and RT scheduling belong on a dedicated thread, or on a later runtime facility. post and submit throw after shutdown. If a task fails, get() on the future returned by submit rethrows the task exception. Tasks must own the lifetime of captured objects (prefer capture by value, or shared_ptr) so they do not hold dangling references.

Reasonable additions: A bounded queue and backpressure (block, drop, or fail when the queue is full) Worker thread names and affinity (through OSAL) Simple metrics (queue length, completion count) Do not put these in this component: Actor lifetime and mode (group) switching Periodic pipelines driven by an external tick or trigger A process-level control plane (command services, heartbeat, liveliness) Those belong to a runtime orchestration layer, designed beside thread_pool, not inside the pool itself.

OpenEmber supports three engineering modes: maintain the framework source tree directly, integrate the framework source into an independent product and build together, and—planned—develop against an installed SDK. The first two already have entry points; the third is for later SDK delivery. This page uses the in-tree scripts/ember from the OpenEmber repo; commands follow the current scaffold. Prepare build dependencies first (Linux, C/C++ compiler, CMake, Protobuf). Building Zenoh from source also needs Rust/Cargo. The first build may download dependencies.

Mode 1: maintain framework source Mode 2: product source integration Mode 3: develop with installed SDK Status Available Available (recommended today) Planned, not implemented yet Project root Fork or copy of OpenEmber Your product repo Your node or product repo Framework access Source belongs to your tree; you can edit it Soft-link or submodule the source Install libs, headers, and CMake package Build Framework and business built together Product uses add_subdirectory(openember) find_package(OpenEmber), business builds alone Product code Apps/services/modules inside the tree Under product apps/, packages/, modules/ In your project, linking public SDK interfaces Upgrades Merge upstream yourself and resolve conflicts Bump dependency source, then re-verify Update installed SDK, check compatibility Fit for Deep customization, learning, full-source delivery Current products, multi-model, framework co-debug Later shared SDK, independent nodes, binary delivery Recommended today: Mode 2—soft-link OpenEmber core into the product and build framework + product together. Focus on project layout and public interfaces first; do not require packaging the framework as a standalone SDK yet. Use a submodule when you need a pinned revision or shared repos. In all three modes the product team owns business code; scaffold output is not auto-updated. Current ember new maps to Mode 2; ember new --standalone and ember dist remain future capabilities.

From your fork or source copy, at that repo root: ./scripts/ember menuconfig ./scripts/ember build -j 4 You can also run ./scripts/ember build -j 4 non-interactively for a default config. Validate the environment with existing samples—see Turtle Demo. When building your own product: Add a product entry and CMakeLists.txt under apps/my_device/; shared business libs can live in modules/. add_subdirectory(my_device) in apps/CMakeLists.txt, add a PRODUCT_* switch in apps/Kconfig (e.g. PRODUCT_BUILD_MY_DEVICE), and gate the build with the generated CMake option. Optional services can live under services/ with the same Kconfig/CMake wiring. Add configs/my_device.launch.yaml for processes, args, and restart policy. Build with launch_manager enabled and start your config explicitly: ./build/bin/launch_manager --launch configs/my_device.launch.yaml Product nodes join the launch router as Link clients. Prefer apps/smart_device_demo/ and configs/smart_device.launch.yaml as references; do not rely only on default launch discovery to pick your product. Keep original copyright and license notices. After editing framework and business in one tree, upstream upgrades need your own merge/rebase and verification of affected interfaces and configs.

With openember/ already in the workspace, from its parent directory: ./openember/scripts/ember new my-robot --model host cd my-robot The scaffold soft-links openember/ to the framework tree used to run the command; it does not copy the whole framework. Layout: my-robot/ ├── CMakeLists.txt # product is the real top-level CMake project ├── Kconfig ├── kconfig/applications.Kconfig ├── apps/product_app/ # initial product node ├── modules/ # your modules ├── products/host/ │ ├── product.defconfig # model default build options │ ├── hardware.yaml # hardware placeholder—fill real endpoints │ └── launch.yaml # process runtime config ├── product.default # default model: host ├── scripts/build.sh └── openember/ # framework dependency Product Kconfig includes the framework’s shared kconfig/workspace.Kconfig; the config tools bind the framework path and compose product fragments—you do not copy that file or the full Kconfig script set into the product repo.

From my-robot/: ./openember/scripts/ember genconfig --product host ./openember/scripts/ember build --product host -j 4 For interactive selection, replace the first command with: ./openember/scripts/ember menuconfig --product host Artifacts land in build/host/bin/; the working model config is build/host/.config. The product root CMake builds the framework via add_subdirectory(openember), then your apps—no separate framework-only build first.

./openember/scripts/ember run --product host --dry-run ./openember/scripts/ember run --product host The first only prints the start command; the second runs launch_manager, which brings up a local router and then product nodes. Default endpoint is tcp/127.0.0.1:7447—ensure no conflicting instance is running. You should see the product app start and heartbeat logs. The initial binary is build/host/bin/openember_my_robot_app, heartbeat topic /nodes/my_robot_app/heartbeat. That only proves wiring and process liveness; the template has no robot control logic or real hardware endpoints. Ctrl+C ends the run. Your nodes should handle SIGINT/SIGTERM, stop workers, release devices, and call openember::Shutdown() in the main loop; forced kill by the supervisor is not a substitute for business cleanup.

Soft-links are fine for co-debug on one machine; changing the link target immediately affects the product build. For shared repos or delivery, prefer a pinned submodule. Example from the workspace parent: ./openember/scripts/ember new my-device --model host --no-symlink cd my-device # --no-symlink leaves an access note only; remove it, then add the submodule rm openember/README.md rmdir openember git init git submodule add https://github.com/openember/openember.git openember Check out the framework commit already validated for the product, then commit the submodule pointer. Teammates should git clone --recurse-submodules. Do not record one revision text while still compiling another source tree. Beyond the framework, also record openember-msgs, third-party libs, external SDKs, and toolchain versions; message-source options are covered in Build OpenEmber. After bumping deps, rebuild and run product tests.

The goal is to install OpenEmber core first, then develop nodes or products against installed headers, libraries, and CMake package config—without embedding or rebuilding framework source in the app workspace. The experience is similar to a ROS install env plus an app workspace, but that does not mean ROS compatibility or adopting its full package/build system. Illustrative target usage—a complete installable SDK workflow is not available yet: cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.16) project(my_node LANGUAGES CXX) find_package(OpenEmber CONFIG REQUIRED) add_executable(my_node main.cpp) target_link_libraries(my_node PRIVATE openember::core) The SDK should export CMake targets that carry public include paths, compile requirements, and link deps so developers do not hand-stitch internal framework paths. Product-specific messages and drivers stay in the product project. Later delivery should distinguish: Dev SDK: public headers, libraries, generated headers, public message bindings, CMake package config, and required transitive deps. Runtime components: libraries needed to run apps, plus optional launch_manager and system services. Starting a node connects to a configured runtime/router; installing the SDK does not auto-start them. Shipping this mode still needs install/export rules, a discoverable OpenEmberConfig.cmake, version/ABI policy, dependency version management, and build/run verification outside the framework source tree. The SDK must match target arch and toolchain. For now only record the mode and boundaries; keep using Mode 2 for product work without changing the current build flow.

documents.t: Add apps/my_service/ and add_subdirectory(apps/my_service) from the product root CMake. Minimal build: add_executable(my_service main.cpp) target_link_libraries(my_service PRIVATE openember::core) set_target_properties(my_service PROPERTIES RUNTIME_OUTPUT_DIRECTORY "${CMAKE_BINARY_DIR}/bin") add_dependencies(openember_product my_service) main.cpp uses openember::Init, CreateNode, and Node pub/sub, Service/Client APIs. Initial apps/product_app/main.cpp is a wiring reference; communication concepts are in OpenEmber Link. Append the process under nodes in products/host/launch.yaml: - name: my_service kind: service command: ${openember.bin}/my_service args: ["--client"] restart: on-failure restart_limit: 3 shutdown_timeout_ms: 3000 heartbeat_timeout_ms: 5000 --client must be parsed by the program. Publish /nodes/my_service/heartbeat with node_name matching launch. Tools without heartbeat can set heartbeat_timeout_ms: 0 to disable supervision for that process. When a build switch disables a node, remove it from launch as well.

Create packages/my_interfaces/ at the product root and add it from top-level CMake. Inside the package you can use: openember_add_proto_library( TARGET my_interfaces ALIAS my_robot::interfaces PROTOS proto/status.proto) Consumers link my_robot::interfaces for generated headers and Protobuf. To import public messages, take OPENEMBER_PROTO_ROOT from openember::msgs_proto, pass it as IMPORT_DIRS, and link openember::msgs_cpp. Keep product-specific messages in the product repo; promote shared protocols to the public message repo when ready.

Enable Hardware Interface and required components, implement adapters in a product package, register factories via EndpointRegistry, and pass the registry to HardwareInterfaceApp. Link openember::hardware_interface so the framework publishes device state and diagnostics. Existing IImu implementations can reuse the shared IMU endpoint through public MakeImuEndpoint. Model protocols, vendor SDKs, calibration, and device paths belong to the product; new product drivers must not require editing built-in framework factory branches. Steps and contracts: upstream hardware endpoint extension. Generated hardware.yaml is only a placeholder—filling device paths does not auto-load drivers; the program must read config, register, and start endpoints.

Add model dirs under products/, each with its own product.defconfig, hardware.yaml, and launch.yaml, then select and build: ./openember/scripts/ember menuconfig --product robot-a ./openember/scripts/ember build --product robot-a -j 4 ./openember/scripts/ember run --product robot-a --dry-run Share business code, keep config per model, isolate artifacts under build/<model>/. Explicit --product is the clearest; without it tools reuse the selected model, initially from product.default. Full split between build options and module runtime parameters: Build configuration and runtime parameters. Kconfig decides which capabilities participate in the build; product options use PRODUCT_* (often in kconfig/applications.Kconfig) and export as same-named CMake variables. launch YAML decides which processes run, args, and supervision. hardware YAML is interpreted by the hardware program for device instances and endpoints. Rebuild after config changes. ember defconfig --product host resets that model’s working config (backed up as .config.pre-defconfig); editing an existing model’s default file does not automatically overwrite its working .config.

Finish no-hardware bring-up, messaging, exit, and fault tests before real devices. Whole-machine state machines, cyclic control, safety, policy, and deployment stay on the product side—framework process heartbeats do not replace device readiness or control authorization. More boundaries: upstream product scaffold and variants and runtime supervision and product app.

Status: Draft / Experimental Specification version: 1.0 RBU: Robot Bundle Update RBU (Robot Bundle Update) is a multi-component release description and update-bundle format for robots and complex intelligent devices. A robot rarely has a single software version. It is a set of independently updatable components: a Linux system, applications, system services, a PMU, a BMS, motors, sensors, and more. RBU describes that set in a format that is simple, transparent, and verifiable: The software state a product Release should finally be in, and which Artifacts are required to bring a device to that state. RBU 1.0 is intentionally small. It does not try to define an update protocol for every device, and it does not replace RAUC, SWUpdate, Mender, or a vendor Bootloader or Firmware Updater. RBU defines only the robot-level Release Contract + Bundle Format.

RBU 1.0 follows these principles: Simple: the format is small enough that a developer can implement a Reader, a Builder, and a Verifier quickly. Transparent: an update bundle is not a black box. It can be unpacked and inspected as manifest.json plus Artifacts. Offline First: RBU does not depend on a cloud. It can be delivered as a local file, over USB, through a Web Console, or over a local network. Multi-component: one Release can describe Linux, applications, services, and several MCU or peripheral firmware images at once. Desired State: a Release describes the complete software state the target device should reach. Extensible: RBU 1.0 defines only the minimum core. Later versions can add signatures, an instance model, dependencies, and transactions. Implementation Independent: RBU does not require a particular language, database, GUI, OTA Agent, or cloud platform.

This document uses the following keywords for requirements: MUST: an implementation has to satisfy this, or it is not RBU 1.0. MUST NOT: an implementation must not behave this way. SHOULD: strongly recommended. Depart from it only with a clear understanding of the consequences. SHOULD NOT: generally not recommended. MAY: an optional capability.

The full RBU architecture can be read as seven layers, but RBU 1.0 does not require users to operate seven models directly. Term Chinese RBU 1.0 Release Model 发布模型 / 整机发布模型 Core Component Model 组件模型 Core Instance Model 实例模型 / 设备实例模型 Not standardized yet Artifact Model 制品模型 / 构建制品模型 Core Bundle Model 升级包模型 Core Execution Model 升级执行模型 handler / order / reboot_after Security Model 安全模型 Integrity verification For an ordinary RBU user, the only relationship the first version requires is: Release │ ├── Component A ── Artifact A ├── Component B ── Artifact B └── Component C ── Artifact C │ ▼ RBU Bundle

A Release is the complete target software state of a product: the Desired State. For example: D50_HW1C1 Release 1.0.0 │ ├── Linux Image 1.0.0 ├── OpenEmber 1.0.0 ├── PMU Firmware 1.0.0 ├── BMS Firmware 1.0.0 └── Motor Firmware 1.0.0 Here: 1.0.0 is the whole-product Product Release Version; each Component also has its own version (they happen to be 1.0.0 above; a real product may use 0.8.2, 2.0.1, and so on); the two levels are different and must not be conflated. One important rule of RBU 1.0: A Release always describes the complete Desired State, not "the files this particular update happens to carry". So even when an Incremental RBU carries only one BMS firmware image, the Manifest still describes every Component Version of the target Release.

A Component is a logical software or firmware unit with its own version lifecycle. For example: system openember pmu bms motor A Component is not the same thing as a file: Component: bms Version: 1.0.1 Artifact: bms_app_v1001.bin The next update may become: Component: bms Version: 1.0.2 Artifact: bms_app_v1002.bin The Component ID stays bms.

id: MUST be a stable logical identifier; MUST be unique within one Manifest; SHOULD be a short, machine-readable string; SHOULD NOT encode a version, filename, or hardware address that is likely to change. Recommended: system openember pmu motor Not recommended: pmu-v1000 motor-can0-node3

version MUST be a non-empty string. RBU 1.0 does not require Semantic Versioning. An implementation SHOULD use SemVer when it can, for example: 1.0.0 2.1.3 0.8.2 An RBU Reader must not assume that every vendor version is SemVer.

A robot may contain several real device instances of the same kind. A quadruped, for example, may have 12 motors: motor ├── FL-Hip ├── FL-Thigh ├── FL-Calf ├── FR-Hip ├── ... └── RR-Calf RBU 1.0 does not standardize a general Instance Topology. If a group of devices: uses the same firmware; uses the same update strategy; and the Update Handler can enumerate and update those instances itself; then a single Component is enough: motor 1.0.0 The Handler is responsible for applying that firmware to every target motor. If a later project needs different firmware, a different Hardware Revision, or independent Target Selection per instance, a later RBU version can introduce a general Instance Model.

An Artifact is a file that an RBU Bundle actually carries and delivers. For example: OpenEmber_D50_1.0.0.zip openember-1.0.0-arm64-D50_HW1C1.tar.gz pmu_app_v1000.bin bms_app_v1000.bin motor_app_v1000.bin RBU treats an Artifact as an Opaque Artifact. OpenEmber_D50_1.0.0.zip might contain: OpenEmber_D50_1.0.0.zip ├── boot.img ├── manifest.json ├── MiniLoaderAll.bin ├── misc.img ├── package-file ├── parameter.txt ├── rootfs.img ├── rootfs.img.sha256 ├── uboot.img └── userdata.img To RBU, the whole ZIP is still one Artifact: Component: system Artifact: OpenEmber_D50_1.0.0.zip RBU does not define: how boot.img is flashed; which partition rootfs.img maps to; how uboot.img is updated; how the ZIP's own manifest.json is interpreted. Those belong to a concrete System Update Handler or to the underlying OTA system.

An Artifact that the Bundle actually carries MUST include: { "path": "artifacts/bms_app_v1001.bin", "size": 262144, "sha256": "..." } Field definitions: Field Type Required Description path string MUST Relative path of the Artifact inside the RBU size integer MUST Exact size of the file in bytes sha256 string MUST SHA-256 of the file contents, 64 hexadecimal characters path: MUST be under artifacts/; MUST be a relative path; MUST NOT contain .. path traversal; MUST NOT be an absolute path.
RBU 1.0 defines two Bundle types: full incremental
A .rbu MUST be: USTAR archive + Zstandard compression Recommended extension: .rbu RBU does not use a private binary container. The point is to stay transparent and easy to implement.

Standard layout: bundle.rbu ├── manifest.json └── artifacts/ ├── component-a.bin └── component-b.tar.gz Requirements: manifest.json MUST sit at the archive root; every carried Artifact MUST live under artifacts/; every Artifact referenced by the Manifest MUST exist; artifacts/ SHOULD NOT contain files the Manifest does not reference.
An RBU 1.0 Manifest is UTF-8 JSON. Top-level structure: { "spec": "rbu/1.0", "release": {}, "bundle": {}, "components": [] }
MUST be: "rbu/1.0" A consumer MUST reject an RBU major version it does not support.

{ "product": "D50_HW1C1", "version": "1.0.0" } Field Required Description product MUST Stable identifier of the target product or SKU version MUST Target Product Release Version release identifies the complete Desired State. It does not describe how the Bundle is transported.

Full Bundle: { "type": "full" } Incremental Bundle: { "type": "incremental", "from_release": "1.0.0" } Field Required Description type MUST full or incremental from_release MUST for incremental Base Release that an incremental bundle is allowed to update created_at MAY Bundle build time; ISO 8601 UTC is recommended tool MAY Builder name, version, and similar information

Every Component MUST contain at least: { "id": "bms", "version": "1.0.1", "handler": "openember.bms", "order": 400 } Field definitions: Field Type Required Description id string MUST Stable Component ID version string MUST Target version in the Target Release handler string MUST Update Handler identifier order integer MUST Minimum execution-order hint; a smaller value runs earlier reboot_after boolean MAY Whether a successful install forms a reboot barrier; see section 12.3 artifact object Conditional Present when this Bundle actually carries the component order SHOULD be unique within one Manifest. An implementation must not rely on an implicit order between equal order values. If reboot_after is omitted, the meaning is false.

A Full Bundle is the complete Artifact set of the target Release. For example: D50_HW1C1_1.0.0_full.rbu For a Full Bundle: bundle.type MUST be full; the Manifest MUST describe the complete target Component state; every Component listed in the Manifest MUST include artifact; the corresponding Artifact file MUST exist under artifacts/. A Full Bundle is typically used for: factory install; field or service recovery; a cross-version upgrade; a downgrade; a device whose current software state is unknown. Whether an upgrade or a downgrade is actually allowed is still decided by the concrete Handler and by product policy.

An RBU 1.0 Incremental Bundle is a component-level delta (Component-level Delta), not a Binary Delta. For example: D50_HW1C1 1.0.0 → 1.0.1 Only changed: BMS 1.0.0 → 1.0.1 The .rbu then only needs to carry: manifest.json artifacts/ └── bms_app_v1001.bin The Manifest MUST still describe the complete Desired State of 1.0.1. For an Incremental Bundle: bundle.type MUST be incremental; bundle.from_release MUST be present; the Manifest MUST describe every Component of the target Release; an added or changed Component MUST carry an Artifact; an unchanged Component SHOULD NOT carry an Artifact; an Agent MUST NOT apply the Bundle to a device that does not satisfy from_release. This split keeps two ideas apart: Release = complete Desired State Bundle = the payload required to bring the device to that Desired State

The minimum execution metadata in RBU 1.0 is: handler order reboot_after Of these: handler and order decide who installs, and in what order; reboot_after decides whether a successful Component forms a reboot barrier, and whether later Components continue after the reboot.

handler is an implementation-defined Update Handler identifier, for example: openember.system-image openember.package openember.pmu openember.bms openember.motor RBU 1.0 does not define a global Handler Registry, and it does not specify the internal behavior of a Handler. A Handler owns the concrete update mechanism, for example: Linux A/B or partition flashing; Debian package installation; tar or zip package installation; CAN / CAN FD; UART; RS485; Ethernet; a Bootloader protocol; a Component Version Probe; post-install verification; triggering a reboot; Rollback. Therefore: RS485 is a transport, not a complete Handler. Even if PMU and BMS are both updated over RS485, they may still use entirely different bootloaders and update protocols.

order is an integer execution-order hint: 100 System 200 OpenEmber 300 PMU 400 BMS 500 Motor A Component with a smaller value SHOULD run first. RBU 1.0 does not define: depends_on before / after transaction_group phase graph If a later project shows that a single order cannot express real dependencies, a later specification can extend it.

Robot updates often reboot after a system image or a critical runtime is updated, then continue installing firmware or other components. RBU 1.0 uses the Component-level boolean reboot_after to declare a reboot barrier, so a Manifest can express "install this component → reboot → continue with later components". Allowed values: Value Meaning false No reboot barrier (the default; the field may be omitted) true After this Component completes successfully, the device MUST reboot before any Component with a larger order runs, and execution MUST continue after the reboot Example: { "id": "system", "version": "1.0.0", "handler": "openember.system-image", "order": 100, "reboot_after": true } Required semantics: The Agent MUST execute Components that need to be installed in ascending order. When an executed Component has reboot_after set to true and the install succeeds, the Agent MUST treat it as a reboot barrier in the execution plan: reboot before continuing to later Components. After the reboot, the Agent MUST resume at the unfinished Components after that barrier. It MUST NOT unconditionally rerun the whole Bundle from the start. If a Component is skipped in this plan (for example an unchanged Component in an Incremental Bundle that was not actually installed), its reboot_after SHOULD NOT raise a reboot barrier. One Manifest MAY contain several reboot_after: true entries. Each barrier that runs successfully takes effect on its own. RBU 1.0 defines only the Manifest semantics above. It does not specify implementation details such as: how the reboot is initiated (Agent, Handler, or Bootloader); where progress or checkpoints are stored (a file, a database, A/B metadata, and so on); reboot timeout, failure retry, or power-loss recovery; how an unfinished Bundle is rediscovered after reboot. Those are responsibilities of a concrete RBU Agent.
The minimum security capability of RBU 1.0 is Artifact Integrity Verification.

For every Artifact the Bundle carries: size MUST match the actual file length in bytes; sha256 MUST match the actual SHA-256 of the file; the Agent or Verifier MUST verify integrity before install. A Verifier MUST reject: a missing manifest.json; a Manifest whose JSON cannot be parsed; an unsupported spec; a missing Artifact; an Artifact size mismatch; an Artifact SHA-256 mismatch; an illegal Artifact path; a Manifest that clearly violates Full or Incremental Bundle semantics.

SHA-256 can detect accidental corruption, or a file that does not match the Manifest. It cannot prove that a trusted publisher signed the Bundle. If an attacker can modify both: Artifact + manifest.json and recompute the SHA-256, a hash alone does not stop that attack. Digital signatures are therefore an important security feature for a later RBU version. The RBU 1.0 draft does not yet define: an Ed25519 or ECDSA signature format; Public Key Distribution; certificates; Key Rotation; TPM or HSM; Online Authorization. A later version can add them without breaking the current Bundle Layout, for example: bundle.rbu ├── manifest.json ├── manifest.sig └── artifacts/

RBU tracks software state through Version plus Artifact. A Builder or Release Tool SHOULD prevent this: BMS 1.0.1 SHA256 = AAAA... followed later by: BMS 1.0.1 SHA256 = BBBB... If the Component Version is unchanged and the Artifact content has changed, the release tool SHOULD reject a formal build and require a Component Version bump. Recommended rule: Version same + SHA same → Same Artifact Version changed + SHA changed → Normal Change Version same + SHA changed → Error This check belongs mainly to the Release Tool or Builder. Every RBU tool is strongly encouraged to implement it.

documents.t: The example product D50_HW1C1 is the RBU 1.0 reference example. In this example, OpenEmber runtime software (the application, Web Console, OTA Agent, and similar pieces) is packaged as one product-software Component, openember, rather than as several independent deb or tar packages.

OpenEmber_D50_1.0.0.zip openember-1.0.0-arm64-D50_HW1C1.tar.gz pmu_app_v1000.bin bms_app_v1000.bin motor_app_v1000.bin Corresponding Desired State: Product: D50_HW1C1 Release: 1.0.0 Linux Image 1.0.0 OpenEmber 1.0.0 PMU Firmware 1.0.0 BMS Firmware 1.0.0 Motor Firmware 1.0.0

Recommended filename: D50_HW1C1_1.0.0_full.rbu Layout: D50_HW1C1_1.0.0_full.rbu ├── manifest.json └── artifacts/ ├── OpenEmber_D50_1.0.0.zip ├── openember-1.0.0-arm64-D50_HW1C1.tar.gz ├── pmu_app_v1000.bin ├── bms_app_v1000.bin └── motor_app_v1000.bin Example Manifest: { "spec": "rbu/1.0", "release": { "product": "D50_HW1C1", "version": "1.0.0" }, "bundle": { "type": "full" }, "components": [ { "id": "system", "version": "1.0.0", "handler": "openember.system-image", "order": 100, "reboot_after": true, "artifact": { "path": "artifacts/OpenEmber_D50_1.0.0.zip", "size": 0, "sha256": "<sha256>" } }, { "id": "openember", "version": "1.0.0", "handler": "openember.package", "order": 200, "artifact": { "path": "artifacts/openember-1.0.0-arm64-D50_HW1C1.tar.gz", "size": 0, "sha256": "<sha256>" } }, { "id": "pmu", "version": "1.0.0", "handler": "openember.pmu", "order": 300, "artifact": { "path": "artifacts/pmu_app_v1000.bin", "size": 0, "sha256": "<sha256>" } }, { "id": "bms", "version": "1.0.0", "handler": "openember.bms", "order": 400, "artifact": { "path": "artifacts/bms_app_v1000.bin", "size": 0, "sha256": "<sha256>" } }, { "id": "motor", "version": "1.0.0", "handler": "openember.motor", "order": 500, "artifact": { "path": "artifacts/motor_app_v1000.bin", "size": 0, "sha256": "<sha256>" } } ] } size: 0 and <sha256> in the example are documentation placeholders. A real Builder MUST use the Artifact's actual byte length and SHA-256. Here system sets "reboot_after": true, which means the device reboots after the Linux image installs successfully, then continues with openember, firmware, and the remaining components. How the Agent persists progress and resumes after reboot is outside this specification.

Assume: Robot Release: 1.0.0 → 1.0.1 BMS: 1.0.0 → 1.0.1 The other Components are unchanged. Recommended filename: D50_HW1C1_1.0.0_to_1.0.1.rbu Actual Bundle contents: D50_HW1C1_1.0.0_to_1.0.1.rbu ├── manifest.json └── artifacts/ └── bms_app_v1001.bin The Manifest still describes the complete Desired State: { "spec": "rbu/1.0", "release": { "product": "D50_HW1C1", "version": "1.0.1" }, "bundle": { "type": "incremental", "from_release": "1.0.0" }, "components": [ { "id": "system", "version": "1.0.0", "handler": "openember.system-image", "order": 100, "reboot_after": true }, { "id": "openember", "version": "1.0.0", "handler": "openember.package", "order": 200 }, { "id": "pmu", "version": "1.0.0", "handler": "openember.pmu", "order": 300 }, { "id": "bms", "version": "1.0.1", "handler": "openember.bms", "order": 400, "artifact": { "path": "artifacts/bms_app_v1001.bin", "size": 0, "sha256": "<sha256>" } }, { "id": "motor", "version": "1.0.0", "handler": "openember.motor", "order": 500 } ] }

The RBU specification defines format and semantics. It does not require a product to implement its toolchain in a particular way. A typical architecture: Release Builder │ ▼ .rbu │ ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐ │ │ │ USB Web Upload Cloud │ │ │ └─────────────┼─────────────┘ ▼ RBU Agent │ Parse / Verify │ Create Plan │ Execute by Handler

collect Component Artifacts; maintain the complete Release Desired State; compare the Base Release and the Target Release; compute Artifact size; compute SHA-256; generate manifest.json; build Full and Incremental RBUs; after the build, read the Bundle back and Verify it.

read the Manifest; check Product and Release compatibility; verify Artifact size and SHA-256; look up an Update Handler from handler; build a minimal execution plan from order and reboot_after, including reboot barriers; persist execution progress when needed, so work can continue after a reboot; call the Handler to perform the actual update.

To keep the specification small, the following are outside the RBU 1.0 core: the internal format of a Linux system Artifact; Partition Layout; PMU or BMS Bootloader protocols; CAN / CAN FD firmware protocols; UART / RS485 firmware protocols; Device Instance Topology; Fleet Management; Cloud OTA; a Device Registry; a SQLite or other database schema; a Builder GUI; Binary Delta; a dependency graph; distributed transactions; a complete Rollback model; digital signatures and PKI; how a reboot is triggered, where a progress checkpoint is stored, or how power-loss recovery works (the Manifest only declares reboot_after semantics). A concrete implementation may provide these on its own. A future RBU version may standardize the ones that prove generally useful.
documents.s: 17. What RBU 1.0 explicitly does not define

documents.t: An RBU Manifest MUST use: "spec": "rbu/1.0" as its format version. An RBU Reader: MUST check spec; MUST reject a major version it cannot understand safely; SHOULD ignore a field it does not recognize when that field is clearly an optional extension, rather than failing only because an optional field was added. The evolution rule is: Prove the problem in a real project first, then add a capability to the specification only if it has general value. Capabilities that may appear later: RBU 1.x ├── Digital Signature ├── Rich Compatibility Rules ├── Artifact Metadata Extension └── Handler Metadata Extension Future ├── Instance Model ├── Dependency / Phase Model ├── Rollback Capability ├── Health Check Contract └── Security / Key Model These are reserved extensions. They are not mandatory in RBU 1.0.

RBU 1.0 can be reduced to one sentence: RBU = Release Manifest + Component Artifacts + Handler Contract + Reboot Continue + Integrity Verification. The core data relationship is: Product Release Desired State │ ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐ │ │ │ Component Component Component system openember motor 1.0.0 1.0.0 1.0.0 │ │ │ Artifact Artifact Artifact │ │ │ └───────────────┼───────────────┘ ▼ RBU Bundle manifest + artifacts │ ▼ Agent │ handler + order + reboot_after + hash │ ▼ Desired State RBU 1.0 does not try to solve every robot OTA problem at once. It establishes a contract that is small enough, clear enough, and concrete enough to implement and use.

Simple beats clever Consistency beats personal preference Clear interfaces beat implementation tricks Design for embedded / SDK / cross-platform use
Use snake_case consistently in C. This is the core decision.

int ember_connect(void); int ember_send_packet(const uint8_t *data, size_t length); void ember_disconnect(void); Rules: All lowercase Separate words with _ Must use a module prefix (very important) Recommended prefixes: ember_* eb_*
int packet_count; uint8_t buffer_size; snake_case Short and clear
int g_packet_count; Use the g_ prefix Prefer to avoid globals
#define EMBER_MAX_PACKET_SIZE 1024 #define EMBER_TIMEOUT_MS 1000 ALL_CAPS with _ Must include a module prefix

For type names, pick PascalCase or snake_case and stick to one project-wide style. We recommend PascalCase (closer to C++): typedef struct { uint8_t *data; size_t length; } EmberPacket; Enumerations: typedef enum { EMBER_STATE_DISCONNECTED, EMBER_STATE_CONNECTING, EMBER_STATE_CONNECTED } EmberState; Enumerators must be ALL_CAPS Include a module prefix

C has no namespaces; naming discipline is what keeps large C codebases sane. One prefix per module Module Prefix core ember_ transport ember_transport_ protocol ember_proto_ Example: int ember_transport_init(void); int ember_transport_send(const uint8_t *data, size_t len);
snake_case ember.c ember_transport.c ember_protocol.c packet_parser.c

Do not expose internal details (approximate “encapsulation”) typedef struct EmberClient EmberClient; struct EmberClient { int socket_fd; int state; }; Or, going further (recommended for SDKs): typedef struct EmberClient EmberClient; EmberClient* ember_create(void); void ember_destroy(EmberClient* client); This enables a lightweight “pseudo-OOP” style.
int ember_connect(void); // 0 = success, <0 = error Recommended: 0 for success Negative values for error codes
int ember_receive(uint8_t *buffer, size_t *length); ✔ Use pointers to return data ✔ Avoid returning large structs by value (better for embedded)
bool is_connected; bool has_error; Functions: bool ember_is_connected(void); ✔ Prefer is_, has_, can_ prefixes
Avoid: int Connect(); // ❌ C++-style name int getCount(); // ❌ camelCase Avoid missing prefixes: int send_packet(); // ❌ pollutes the global namespace Avoid cryptic abbreviations: int pkt_cnt; // ❌
#ifndef EMBER_TRANSPORT_H #define EMBER_TRANSPORT_H // ... #endif ✔ Guard macro name matches the file name in UPPER_SNAKE_CASE

// ember_client.h #ifndef EMBER_CLIENT_H #define EMBER_CLIENT_H #include <stddef.h> #include <stdint.h> #include <stdbool.h> typedef struct EmberClient EmberClient; EmberClient* ember_create(void); void ember_destroy(EmberClient* client); int ember_connect(EmberClient* client); int ember_disconnect(EmberClient* client); int ember_send_packet(EmberClient* client, const uint8_t* data, size_t length); bool ember_is_connected(const EmberClient* client); #endif
Project-wide consistency beats individual habit API readability comes first Names should express meaning, not implementation detail
Use PascalCase, for example: class EmberClient; struct PacketHeader; enum class ConnectionState;

lowerCamelCase (similar to Qt) void connectToServer(); void sendPacket(); int calculateChecksum(); Do not treat public vs. private differently Do not use PascalCase for functions (keeps the style simpler than Google’s mix)
int packetCount() const; void setPacketCount(int count); bool isConnected() const; Same convention as other member functions Avoid Google-style “exception” rules for accessors

Locals / parameters​ int packetCount; std::string deviceName; Member variables​ m_ prefix + camelCase class Client { private: int m_packetCount; bool m_connected; }; Global variables​ int g_packetCount;
PascalCase (no k prefix) const int MaxPacketSize = 1024;
#define EMBER_MAX_BUFFER 1024
snake_case ember_client.h packet_parser.cpp connection_manager.h Why: Works across platforms (Linux / Windows) Avoids case-sensitivity issues
class PacketParser; // parsing only class Connection; // connection only
client.connectToServer(); client.sendPacket(data); client.disconnect(); Avoid: client.DoConnect(); client.HandlePacket();
bool isConnected(); bool hasError(); bool canRetry(); Do not: bool connected(); // ambiguous
enum class ConnectionState { Disconnected, Connecting, Connected, }; PascalCase type name Enumerators without redundant prefixes (avoid STATE_CONNECTED-style noise)
Do not mix styles: get_packet_count() // ❌ GetPacketCount() // ❌ packetCount() // ✅ Do not use meaningless abbreviations: pktCnt // ❌ Do not use type-prefix Hungarian notation: int iCount; // ❌

apps/turtle_demo is a turtlesim-style demo for x86 Linux hosts. It needs no target board or real hardware. Two processes show OpenEmber multi-node Link, Protobuf messages, and optional launch orchestration. An SDL2 window is the default view; use --no-gui when headless. This lives under the Application layer (apps/), not as a tiny API sample in examples/. For full runtime supervision (health / device / config), see smart_device_demo and configs/smart_device.launch.yaml.

This demo mirrors classic ROS turtlesim: think of it as a mobile robot on a plane, not a real car or a 3D simulator. 2D only: pose is (x, y, \theta); the window shows a grid and turtle. No 3D scene. Kinematics: closer to a unicycle / differential-drive model—commanded by linear and angular velocity; no wheels, suspension, Ackermann steering, or physics collisions. Purpose: practice multi-node messaging (topics / Link / msgs), not vehicle or Gazebo-class simulation. For 3D visualization or real robot models, use something like RViz / Gazebo; that is outside the turtlesim tier.
